title: Suite2p: beyond 10,000 neurons with standard two-photon microscopy
authors: Pachitariu M., Stringer C., Dipoppa M., Schröder S., Rossi L.F., Dalgleish H., Carandini M., Harris K.D.
summary: Suite2p is a complete, fast pipeline for two-photon calcium imaging data — registering raw movies to correct for motion, automatically detecting active cells, extracting their fluorescence and neuropil-corrected traces, and deconvolving spike times — built to run faster than real time and recover roughly twice as many cells as prior state-of-the-art methods, with a full GUI for inspecting and curating results.
abstract_long: Suite2p addresses the four core steps of two-photon calcium imaging analysis in one pipeline: registration (correcting for brain motion across frames, including rigid and non-rigid components), cell detection (finding active ROIs directly from the registered movie's statistics rather than requiring a separate structural channel), signal extraction (fluorescence traces per cell, with neuropil contamination subtracted), and spike deconvolution (inferring approximate spike times from the calcium traces). The pipeline runs on standard workstations, processes data faster than real time, and — because it detects cells based on activity rather than static anatomy — recovers substantially more active cells (roughly 2x) than prior approaches, enabling routine detection of well over 10,000 neurons per recording. A companion GUI lets users visually inspect detected ROIs, manually curate the automatic cell/non-cell classification, and explore extracted traces before further analysis.
data_acquisition: Two-photon calcium imaging movies (raw TIFFs or similar), typically from GCaMP-expressing neurons imaged through a cranial window or GRIN lens
animal: Not applicable — general-purpose calcium imaging pipeline, demonstrated on mouse cortex recordings
tutorial_intro: Suite2p expects raw two-photon movie data (TIFF stacks, or several other supported microscope-specific formats) as input — it handles everything from motion correction through to deconvolved spike estimates in one run, either via the GUI or a scriptable Python call.
tutorial_steps: Install with pip install suite2p (add [gui] for the graphical interface: pip install suite2p[gui]), inside a fresh conda environment (Python 3.8+ recommended).

Launch the GUI with python -m suite2p, then use File → Run suite2p to configure a run: point it at your data directory, choose a save path, and set the key acquisition parameters (frame rate, number of imaging planes/channels, expected cell diameter) — or configure and run the same pipeline directly from Python/Jupyter via from suite2p.run_s2p import run_s2p; ops = run_s2p(ops, db), passing your own ops (options) and db (data-location) dictionaries.

The pipeline runs registration (rigid, then optionally non-rigid motion correction), automatic cell detection, and signal extraction with neuropil subtraction, followed by spike deconvolution — all in one pass, with no manual intervention required between steps.

Open the results in the GUI to inspect detected ROIs overlaid on the registered movie, review each ROI's extracted trace, and manually correct the automatic cell/not-cell classification (the classifier's output is stored in iscell.npy, which you can overwrite based on your manual curation).

If registration or cell detection quality looks poor on your first pass, revisit the key parameters (expected cell diameter is the most common one to adjust) and rerun — the GUI displays diagnostic views of the registered movie and mean/max-projection images to help you spot problems (residual motion, wrong diameter estimate) quickly.
tutorial_output: A results folder containing F.npy (per-ROI fluorescence traces), Fneu.npy (matched neuropil traces), spks.npy (deconvolved spike estimates), stat.npy (per-ROI statistics — position, shape, etc.), iscell.npy (the cell/not-cell classification, editable in the GUI), and ops.npy (the run's configuration and registration diagnostics) — everything needed for downstream analysis of neural activity or further curation.

sample_data.text: Suite2p can be tried without a local install via a Google Colab notebook (linked from the repo), which includes example two-photon movies to run the full pipeline.

title: CHIPS: an Extensible Toolbox for Cellular and Hemodynamic Two-Photon Image Analysis
authors: Barrett M.J.P., Ferrari K.D., Stobart J.L., Holub M., Weber B.
summary: CHIPS is a MATLAB toolbox that integrates the full two-photon image-analysis pipeline — import, pre-processing (motion correction, spectral unmixing, denoising), processing, and plotting — for measuring blood vessel diameter, red blood cell velocity, and cellular activity from line-scan or full-frame two-photon microscopy images, designed to be usable with little programming experience while remaining fully scriptable for advanced users.
abstract_long: Two-photon microscopy produces more functional imaging data than can be analyzed manually, but published analysis algorithms are often hard to combine into one workflow: extracting metadata is tedious, pre-processing steps like motion correction or spectral unmixing must be bolted on separately, code may not run across platforms or MATLAB versions, and running several algorithms for the same analysis type usually means maintaining several disparate pipelines. CHIPS (Cellular and Hemodynamic Image Processing Suite) addresses this by wrapping import, pre-processing, processing, and plotting into one set of MATLAB classes built around common analysis types — line-scan or cross-sectional blood vessel diameter, red-blood-cell velocity from line scans, and cellular activity from a wide range of functional indicators. It auto-extracts metadata from ScanImage TIFFs or any OME Bio-Formats-compatible file, includes pre-processing helpers (whole-frame or line-by-line motion correction, spectral unmixing, channel combination for FRET ratios, denoising), runs its algorithms without interaction (many parallelized, either within an algorithm or across an array of images), and ships a GUI for interactive parameter optimization plus built-in plots and CSV export. Its modular, class-based design is intended to make it straightforward for developers to add new analysis types or alternative algorithms for existing ones.
data_acquisition: Two-photon microscopy images of cells and blood vessels — line scans or full-frame images, primarily ScanImage TIFF or any OME Bio-Formats-compatible format
animal: Not applicable — general-purpose toolbox for two-photon image analysis, demonstrated in rodent brain imaging
tutorial_intro: CHIPS is organized around a small set of analysis classes, one per image/analysis type — for example LineScanVel for line-scan red-blood-cell velocity, LineScanDiam for line-scan vessel diameter, XSectScan for full-frame vessel cross-sectional diameter, or CellScan for cellular activity — each following the same import → pre-process → process → plot/output workflow.
tutorial_steps: Download the self-contained MATLAB toolbox from the GitHub repo and add it to your MATLAB path (works on Windows, macOS, and Linux, MATLAB R2013a or later; no additional MATLAB toolboxes needed in most cases).

Create an object of the analysis class matching your data and question: LineScanVel for RBC velocity from a line scan along a vessel centreline, LineScanDiam for vessel diameter from a line scan across a vessel, XSectScan for vessel diameter from a full-frame cross-section image, or CellScan for cellular activity.

Import your images — CHIPS reads ScanImage TIFF files directly (auto-extracting the relevant metadata) or any format supported by the OME Bio-Formats framework; other image data already loaded into MATLAB via your own scripts can be wrapped with RawImgDummy.

Apply any needed pre-processing methods, such as motion_correct (whole-frame or line-by-line shift correction) and unmix_chs (spectral unmixing to remove fluorophore bleed-through), plus channel combination (for example, building a ratio channel for FRET sensors) or denoising as needed.

Call process to run the core algorithm — this executes without further interaction, and many algorithms are parallelized (across an array of images, or within a single algorithm) for substantial speed-ups on multi-core machines. Where CHIPS offers more than one algorithm for the same analysis type (for example, different cell-activity detection methods), choose the one suited to your indicator and cell type.
Use the built-in opt_config GUI to interactively tune analysis parameters against your own data before running a full batch.

Call plot for the default visualization for your object type (for a LineScanVel, this includes velocity, pixel shift, and estimated SNR traces over time), or use the data-output functions to export the underlying results to CSV for analysis outside MATLAB.

For groups of images, apply the same workflow with shared parameters across nearly identical images (for example, repeated trials from the same location), or with per-image parameter adjustments across similar-but-distinct images — and, within a single image, run separate analyses simultaneously on different regions (for example, a cell's activity and a nearby vessel's diameter together).
tutorial_output: Depending on the analysis class used: blood vessel diameter or red-blood-cell velocity over time (from line-scan or full-frame vessel images), or per-cell activity traces (from calcium or other functional indicators) — each with CHIPS's default diagnostic plots (for example raw pixel shift and estimated SNR alongside the measured quantity) and CSV-exportable underlying data for further analysis.

title: DeepLabCut: markerless pose estimation of user-defined body parts with deep learning
authors: Mathis A., Mamidanna P., Cury K.M., Abe T., Murthy V.N., Mathis M.W., Bethge M.
summary: DeepLabCut is a markerless pose-estimation toolbox that uses transfer learning from networks pretrained on human pose estimation to track user-defined body parts in animals from ordinary video, requiring only a small number of manually labeled frames — since its original 2018 release it has grown into a full ecosystem covering multi-animal tracking, 3D pose, and (via SuperAnimal) pretrained models that work across species with no task-specific training at all.
abstract_long: DeepLabCut adapts a deep neural network architecture originally developed for human pose estimation (based on DeeperCut) to animal tracking via transfer learning: starting from weights pretrained on a large human-pose dataset, the network can be fine-tuned to detect user-defined animal body parts from a relatively small number of hand-labeled training frames (the original paper demonstrated accurate tracking from as few as ~200 labeled frames). The authors validate this on three very different behaviors — trail tracking and reaching in mice, and egg-laying behavior in Drosophila — showing human-level labeling accuracy without any markers or specialized hardware. Since publication, the DeepLabCut ecosystem has expanded considerably: DeepLabCut 2.x added a full Python package and GUI, later work added multi-animal pose estimation and identity tracking, 3D pose reconstruction from multiple cameras, and most recently the SuperAnimal models (Ye et al., 2024), which are pretrained across many species and often work directly on new data with zero additional training.
data_acquisition: Standard video of an animal (or, in later multi-animal versions, several animals) performing a behavior — no markers or specialized hardware required
animal: Demonstrated in mice, Drosophila, and (in later work) many other species; general-purpose via transfer learning
tutorial_intro: DeepLabCut works on any video of an animal performing a behavior. For a completely new setup, expect to label a modest number of frames yourself (the original paper used as few as ~200); if your species/setup resembles one of the SuperAnimal pretrained model's training data, you may be able to skip labeling and training entirely.
tutorial_steps: Install via conda/pip following the instructions in the repo (a GPU is strongly recommended for training, though CPU-only inference is workable for small jobs), or use the provided Docker image or Google Colab notebook to avoid a local install altogether.

Create a new project (deeplabcut.create_new_project(...) in Python, or via the GUI), which sets up a standardized folder structure and lets you define the skeleton — the set of body parts you want to track — for your specific animal/behavior.

Extract and manually label training frames using the built-in labeling GUI: DeepLabCut selects a representative, diverse set of frames from your videos for you to annotate, minimizing labeling effort while maximizing training coverage.

Train the network (deeplabcut.train_network(...)) — thanks to transfer learning from a pretrained backbone, this converges with far fewer labeled frames and less training time than training a pose-estimation network from scratch.

Evaluate the trained model on held-out labeled frames, then run inference on new, unlabeled videos (deeplabcut.analyze_videos(...)) to extract body-part coordinates and confidence scores frame by frame; use the built-in plotting/labeling-video tools to visually confirm tracking quality before trusting the output for downstream analysis.

If you're tracking multiple interacting animals, use the multi-animal project workflow instead (introduced in DeepLabCut 2.2+, described in Lauer et al. 2022), which additionally handles identity assignment across frames. If your species/setup is well covered by an existing SuperAnimal model, try that first via deeplabcut.video_inference_superanimal(...) before investing in your own labeling and training.
tutorial_output: Per-frame, per-body-part (x, y) coordinates with a confidence/likelihood score, saved per video (typically as HDF5/CSV), plus optional labeled videos and trajectory plots for visual quality control — for multi-animal projects, coordinates additionally carry a consistent identity/track assignment across frames.

extra_links.label: Nath, Mathis et al. 2019 (Nature Protocols step-by-step user guide for DeepLabCut 2.x)
Lauer et al. 2022 (multi-animal pose estimation and tracking with DeepLabCut)
SuperAnimal pretrained models (Ye et al., Nat Commun 2024 — zero-shot pose estimation across species)

title: Cell Detection with Star-Convex Polygons
authors: Schmidt U., Weigert M., Broaddus C., Myers G.
summary: StarDist detects and segments cell/nuclei instances in microscopy images by predicting a star-convex polygon per pixel, avoiding the merging and suppression errors common with per-pixel or bounding-box approaches in crowded images — available as a Python package with pretrained 2D/3D models, and as plugins for QuPath, napari, Fiji, Icy, and KNIME.
abstract_long: The authors propose StarDist, a convolutional neural network (based on U-Net) that, for every pixel, predicts a star-convex polygon describing the boundary of the cell instance at that location, plus an object probability score. Non-maximum suppression over these overcomplete polygon candidates yields the final instance segmentation. Compared to per-pixel segmentation followed by connected-component grouping (which merges touching cells) or bounding-box-based detectors like Mask R-CNN (whose axis-aligned boxes overlap heavily and get wrongly suppressed for crowded, irregularly oriented nuclei), star-convex polygons are a much better shape prior for the roughly round shapes typical of cell nuclei. StarDist matches or exceeds Mask R-CNN on a challenging real fluorescence microscopy dataset (DSB2018) with an order of magnitude fewer parameters, and handles crowded/touching nuclei substantially better than pixel-classification baselines.
data_acquisition: Fluorescence and brightfield (H&E) microscopy images of cell nuclei — 2D and 3D
language: Python (core package); Groovy for the QuPath integration
animal: Not applicable — general-purpose nuclei/cell segmentation, not species-specific
tutorial_intro: There are two very different ways to use StarDist depending on whether you want a no-code GUI workflow or a scriptable Python pipeline. If you just want to run a pretrained model on your own microscopy images without writing code, the QuPath extension (linked above as the website/docs) is the easiest path — it's a common way to bring StarDist into digital pathology / histology workflows specifically. If you want to train a custom model, batch-process images programmatically, or work in 3D, use the core Python package directly.
tutorial_steps: QuPath route (no coding): install QuPath, then install the StarDist extension by following the setup instructions on the linked docs page — this involves downloading a compatible pretrained model file (a .pb TensorFlow SavedModel) and pointing QuPath's Groovy script at its location. Once set up, you run nuclei detection directly on images already open in a QuPath project by running the provided detection script, adjusting parameters like pixel size and probability threshold to match your images.

Python route — install: first install TensorFlow (TensorFlow 1 or 2 both work), then pip install stardist (or pip install "stardist[tf1]" if you're on TensorFlow 1). Pre-compiled wheels cover most Linux/Windows/macOS setups; if pip tries to compile from source, you'll need a working C++ compiler (see the repo's troubleshooting section for OS-specific instructions).

Python route — run a pretrained model: from stardist.models import StarDist2D; model = StarDist2D.from_pretrained('2D_versatile_fluo') for fluorescence nuclear-marker images, or '2D_versatile_he' for brightfield H&E histology images. Then labels, _ = model.predict_instances(normalize(img)) (using csbdeep.utils.normalize) gives you a labeled instance mask in one call — no training required if a pretrained model fits your image type.

Python route — train your own model: if your images don't resemble the pretrained model types well, you'll need annotated training data — pairs of raw images and label images where every cell has a distinct integer ID. The repo recommends LabKit (via Fiji, works for 2D or 3D) or QuPath (2D only, using the provided Groovy export script to turn QuPath annotations into StarDist-ready image/mask pairs) for creating these annotations. Once you have annotated pairs, follow the example Jupyter notebooks in the repo's examples/ folder for the full training workflow.

For 3D volumes, the same overall approach extends to predicting star-convex polyhedra instead of 2D polygons (see the companion WACV 2020 paper) — the package and API are largely the same, just with 3D-shaped inputs and models.
tutorial_output: A labeled instance segmentation: every detected cell/nucleus is assigned a unique integer ID in the output mask (0 for background), either as detection objects within your QuPath project (ready for QuPath's built-in measurements and downstream analysis) or as a numpy label array (from the Python API) you can use in your own pipeline. The package also includes a stardist.matching submodule for computing standard instance-segmentation metrics (precision, recall, F1, panoptic quality) between a predicted mask and ground truth, useful for validating a model — pretrained or custom — against your own annotated test images.

sample_data.text: A single test image ships with the Python package (stardist.data.test_image_nuclei_2d()); the training dataset behind the original 2D paper's model is on the GitHub releases page as a zip.

extra_links.label: QuPath annotation export script (build your own training data from QuPath annotations)

title: fMRIPrep: a robust preprocessing pipeline for functional MRI
authors: Esteban O., Markiewicz C.J., Blair R.W., Moodie C.A., Isik A.I., Erramuzpe A., Kent J.D., Goncalves M., DuPre E., et al.
summary: fMRIPrep is an analysis-agnostic preprocessing pipeline for functional MRI that automatically adapts a best-practice workflow (combining FSL, ANTs, FreeSurfer, and AFNI) to the specifics of virtually any BIDS-organized dataset, producing standardized, quality-checked outputs without requiring manual parameter tuning for each new dataset.
abstract_long: Researchers have traditionally built ad hoc fMRI preprocessing workflows for each new dataset, stitching together tools from a large inventory with study-specific parameter choices — a process that's hard to reproduce and easy to get subtly wrong. fMRIPrep instead reads a standard BIDS-organized dataset and automatically configures a "best-in-breed" preprocessing workflow (motion correction, susceptibility distortion correction, coregistration, spatial normalization to standard templates, confound estimation) using established neuroimaging tools under the hood, adapting to whatever acquisition parameters and available data (for example, fieldmaps or their absence) each dataset has. A key design feature is automatically generated visual quality-control reports at defined checkpoints throughout the pipeline, letting researchers quickly spot subject-level problems without manually inspecting every intermediate processing step. The authors show that fMRIPrep introduces less uncontrolled spatial smoothness than commonly used alternative preprocessing pipelines, while requiring far less manual intervention.
data_acquisition: Functional and structural MRI data organized in the BIDS (Brain Imaging Data Structure) standard
language: Python (Nipype workflows, wrapping FSL, ANTs, FreeSurfer, AFNI)
animal: Not applicable — human neuroimaging preprocessing pipeline
tutorial_intro: fMRIPrep requires your data organized as a valid BIDS dataset. It's distributed as a Docker/Singularity container (recommended, since it bundles all underlying dependencies like FreeSurfer, FSL, ANTs, and AFNI at pinned versions) rather than a plain pip-installable package.
tutorial_steps: Organize your raw MRI data into the BIDS format (a directory structure and naming convention for neuroimaging datasets) — this is a prerequisite for fMRIPrep, not something it does for you; tools like the BIDS validator can check your dataset before running.
Obtain a FreeSurfer license file (free for academic use, required since fMRIPrep uses FreeSurfer for surface reconstruction) and place it where the container can find it.

Run fMRIPrep via its Docker image: docker run -ti --rm -v /path/to/bids:/data:ro -v /path/to/output:/out -v /path/to/license.txt:/opt/freesurfer/license.txt nipreps/fmriprep:latest /data /out participant — Singularity is also supported and commonly used on shared HPC clusters where Docker isn't available.

Review the automatically generated HTML quality-control reports (one per subject) before proceeding to your own analysis — these visualize each key processing step (registration accuracy, brain extraction, normalization) so you can quickly flag subjects with problems rather than discovering them downstream.

Use the preprocessed, standardized outputs (and the accompanying confound time series — motion parameters, physiological noise estimates, etc.) as the input to your own statistical analysis pipeline of choice; fMRIPrep deliberately stops at "minimal preprocessing" and does not perform smoothing or statistical modeling itself.
tutorial_output: BIDS-Derivatives-formatted preprocessed functional and structural images (in both subject-native and standard template spaces), a confounds table per run (motion parameters, physiological regressors, and other nuisance variables for use in your own denoising/statistical model), and per-subject HTML visual quality-control reports summarizing every major processing step.

extra_links.label: NiPreps ecosystem (related preprocessing tools: MRIQC, sMRIPrep, dMRIPrep)
BIDS specification (the input data standard fMRIPrep requires)

title: Human Neocortical Neurosolver (HNN), a new software tool for interpreting the cellular and network origin of human MEG/EEG data
authors: Neymotin S.A., Daniels D.S., Caldwell B., McDougal R.A., Carnevale N.T., Jas M., Moore C.I., Hines M.L., Hämäläinen M., Jones S.R.
summary: HNN is a GUI-based biophysical model of a canonical neocortical column that simulates the cellular/circuit origin of human MEG/EEG signals (evoked responses and alpha/beta/gamma rhythms), letting researchers without modeling experience directly compare simulated and recorded current-dipole waveforms to test circuit-level hypotheses.
abstract_long: HNN's core is a model of a canonical layered neocortical column — pyramidal neurons and interneurons arranged across layers, driven by two known input pathways (proximal "feedforward" thalamic drive and distal "feedback" cortico-cortical drive). Because the model simulates the actual intracellular dendritic current flow that generates MEG/EEG signals, its output is in the same units (ampere-meters) as source-localized data, allowing direct one-to-one comparison. The GUI lets users load their own evoked-response or rhythm data, activate the network with user-defined drive parameters, run the simulation, and immediately inspect not just the resulting current dipole but the underlying single-cell spiking and layer-specific activity that produced it — turning parameter tuning into a hypothesis-testing loop. Built-in tutorials reproduce the group's own published findings on tactile evoked responses and alpha/beta/gamma rhythms, including a model-derived prediction about the laminar origin of transient beta events that was later confirmed with invasive recordings in mice and monkeys. Note: the original GUI repository described in this paper is now archived and unmaintained; it has been superseded by hnn-core, a modernized Python package (with its own GUI) that implements the same underlying model and is the version linked here.
data_acquisition: Human non-invasive MEG/EEG (and intracranial ECoG) source-localized current-dipole recordings, compared against a biophysically detailed neocortical circuit simulation
animal: Not applicable — models human MEG/EEG/ECoG; the circuit predictions it generates have separately been validated against laminar recordings in mice and monkeys
tutorial_intro: The tool in this paper (the original HNN GUI) is archived and no longer maintained — install hnn-core instead, which implements the same biophysical model with active support, more features (LFP/CSD simulation, parameter optimization), and its own GUI. The core workflow described below (load data, define network structure, "activate" it with drive parameters, compare to data, inspect microcircuit detail) carries over conceptually from the original paper to hnn-core.
tutorial_steps: Install the Anaconda Python distribution if you don't have it, then create a dedicated environment: conda create -y -q -n hnn-core-env python=3.12, conda activate hnn-core-env, then conda install hnn-core-all -c jonescompneurolab -c conda-forge. (If you'd rather use pip, hnn-core supports Python 3.9 through 3.13 that way — see the Installation Guide linked above for details.)

Alternatively, try HNN in your browser with no local install via Google Colab notebooks or the Neuroscience Gateway Portal — both are linked from the Installation Guide, useful if you just want to explore before committing to a local setup.

Load your MEG/EEG/ECoG data (this step is optional — you can also just explore rhythm generation without comparing to real data) and the default canonical neocortical column network loads automatically; adjust its structure (cell counts, connectivity) if needed.

"Activate" the network by defining layer-specific exogenous drive — proximal drive represents feedforward thalamic input, distal drive represents feedback from higher-order cortex, and both can be single spikes, rhythmic bursts, or Poisson-distributed noisy drive depending on what signal you're trying to reproduce (evoked response vs. oscillation).

Run the simulation and compare the resulting current-dipole waveform to your loaded data (goodness of fit is reported via RMSE), then inspect the underlying layer-specific activity, individual cell spiking, and somatic voltages that produced it to understand the circuit-level story behind the signal.

Iterate: adjust drive timing/strength (by hand, or using HNN's built-in stepwise parameter optimization for evoked responses) to test different circuit hypotheses, and compare across simulated experimental conditions.

For a full click-by-click walkthrough (the original paper's tutorials on evoked responses and alpha/beta/gamma rhythms have modern equivalents), see the HNN Textbook linked above rather than the archived paper-era GUI screenshots.
tutorial_output: The primary output is a simulated current-dipole waveform (in ampere-meters, directly comparable to source-localized MEG/EEG data) for whatever drive parameters you defined, alongside the full microcircuit detail that generated it: individual pyramidal neuron and interneuron spike times, somatic voltages, and layer-specific dipole contributions. For evoked-response fitting, HNN also reports a goodness-of-fit RMSE between simulated and recorded waveforms, and (with hnn-core) supports simulating LFP and current-source-density signals alongside the dipole.

sample_data.text: Example datasets from this paper (tactile evoked responses, spontaneous SI alpha/beta rhythms, and visual gamma rhythms) are bundled with the original software's data folder.

extra_links.label: Original paper-exact GUI (archived, kept only for reproducing this paper)
HNN Textbook (full documentation, tutorials, installation guide)

title: Brain states govern the spatio-temporal dynamics of resting-state functional connectivity
authors: Aedo-Jury F., Schwalm M., Hamzehpour L., Stroh A.
summary: Combining simultaneous fMRI and fiber-photometry calcium recordings in rats, this paper shows that resting-state functional connectivity depends on the brain's current activity state — a compartmentalized, small-world network during persistent activity versus a cortex-wide, randomly connected network during slow wave activity, driven by population down-up transitions — with the full MATLAB connectivity-analysis pipeline (ICA, graph theory, fALFF) released alongside it.
abstract_long: The authors compared two distinct rat cortical activity states — persistent activity and slow wave activity — using simultaneous fMRI and calcium fiber-photometry recordings. Independent component analysis revealed well-compartmentalized resting-state networks (e.g. a default-mode-like network) during persistent activity, but a single cortex-wide component during slow wave activity. Graph-theory analysis showed persistent activity has small-world network properties (high modularity, high clustering), while slow wave activity behaves more like a randomly connected network. This distinction held regardless of which anesthetic agent was used, ruling out an anesthesia-specific confound. Using the pan-cortical slow-wave component as a covariate, and directly correlating fiber-photometry-measured population down-up transitions with BOLD connectivity, the authors show that these transitions are the specific driver of the cortex-wide connectivity increase seen during slow wave activity — arguing that resting-state fMRI studies should account for the brain's underlying activity state rather than treating "rest" as a single condition.
data_acquisition: Simultaneous rat resting-state fMRI (BOLD, 9.4T) and optic-fiber-based calcium photometry recordings, under isoflurane (slow wave activity) or medetomidine (persistent activity) conditions
animal: Rat
tutorial_intro: This is a set of custom MATLAB scripts for the specific connectivity analyses in this paper (ICA-based network identification, cortical-parcellation functional connectivity, graph theory metrics, fALFF, and matrix similarity) rather than a general-purpose installable toolbox — expect to adapt the scripts to your own rs-fMRI + physiology dataset rather than run them unmodified. The ICA step itself depends on a separate, well-established third-party tool (GIFT).
tutorial_steps: Preprocessing (motion correction, smoothing, alignment to an anatomical template) was done in Brain Voyager, a commercial package — you'll need equivalent preprocessing done in whatever software you use (e.g. SPM, AFNI) before these scripts apply, since the repo picks up after that step.

Independent component analysis was run using GIFT (Group ICA of fMRI Toolbox), a free, separately maintained MATLAB toolbox — install that first if you want to reproduce the ICA-based network identification specifically.

The core connectivity analysis parcellates the cortex into regions of interest (this paper used the Valdes-Hernandez rat atlas), extracts the mean BOLD time course per region, and computes a partial-correlation matrix using ventricle/white-matter signal and breathing rate as covariates — adapt the atlas and covariate choices to your own species/setup.

Graph theory metrics (modularity, global/local efficiency, clustering coefficient, characteristic path length) are computed on the resulting adjacency matrices using the Brain Connectivity Toolbox (an established, separately available MATLAB toolbox for network analysis) — check the repo's scripts for how thresholding via FDR correction was applied before computing these metrics.

For relating a physiological "down-up transition" signal (from fiber photometry or any other population-activity readout) to functional connectivity, see the covariate-based analysis and the direct correlation/permutation-test approach described in the Methods — this is the piece most reusable if you have your own dual-modality (imaging + population activity) dataset and want to test whether a specific physiological event type is driving connectivity in the way this paper shows for slow-wave down-up transitions.
tutorial_output: Per-subject functional connectivity matrices (regions × regions), graph-theory metric values (modularity, efficiency, clustering coefficient, path length) per activity state, fALFF power distributions, and matrix-similarity (Frobenius norm) scores for comparing connectivity patterns across conditions — the same building blocks used to generate every figure in the paper.

sample_data.text: All source data underlying the figures are on Dryad.

title: SpikeInterface, a unified framework for spike sorting
authors: Buccino A.P., Hurwitz C.L., Garcia S., Magland J., Siegle J.H., Hurwitz R., Hennig M.H.
summary: SpikeInterface is a Python framework that wraps essentially every popular spike-sorting algorithm (including Kilosort, MountainSort, IronClust, SpyKING CIRCUS, and others) behind one consistent API, so you can read/write dozens of extracellular file formats, preprocess and postprocess recordings, run and directly compare multiple sorters on the same data, compute standard quality metrics, and export curated results to Phy — all without learning each tool's own idiosyncratic interface.
abstract_long: Before SpikeInterface, comparing spike-sorting algorithms meant learning a different, often incompatible tool for each one — complicating reproducible benchmarking and slowing adoption of newer methods. SpikeInterface unifies this landscape: its extractors module reads and writes dozens of recording and sorting file formats (so a recording loaded once works with any wrapped sorter); its preprocessing module handles standard steps like filtering, common referencing, and whitening; its sorters module wraps essentially all popular spike sorters (many packaged for one-line execution via Docker/Singularity, avoiding manual installation of each one's dependencies); its postprocessing and quality-metrics modules compute standard curation statistics (ISI violations, waveform metrics, and more) usable for automatic or manual curation; and its comparison module benchmarks sorter outputs against each other or against ground truth. The authors demonstrate the framework by reproducibly running, comparing, and benchmarking multiple spike sorters on real and simulated datasets with only a few lines of code, substantially reducing the manual-curation burden compared to running each sorter's own native pipeline.
data_acquisition: Extracellular electrophysiology recordings in any common file format (Neuropixels, Open Ephys, Intan, Blackrock, NWB, and many others)
animal: Not applicable — a format- and algorithm-agnostic framework, not tied to a species or acquisition system
tutorial_intro: SpikeInterface expects an extracellular recording in essentially any common electrophysiology format — its extractors handle format conversion, so you generally don't need to convert your data yourself before starting.
tutorial_steps: Install with pip install spikeinterface[full] (the [full] extra pulls in all the optional sub-module dependencies; [full,widgets] additionally adds interactive visualization widgets).

Load your recording with the appropriate extractor for your format, for example recording = se.read_openephys(folder_path) or the equivalent reader for Neuropixels/SpikeGLX, Blackrock, NWB, etc. — the resulting recording object works identically regardless of the original file format.

Apply preprocessing as needed (for example, bandpass filtering and common median referencing) by chaining preprocessing functions on the recording object — each step returns a new lazy recording object, so nothing is computed until you actually run a sorter or write to disk.

Run one or more sorters on the same preprocessed recording via a single consistent call, for example sorting_KS = ss.run_sorter('kilosort4', recording) and sorting_MS = ss.run_sorter('mountainsort5', recording) — many sorters run inside a prebuilt Docker/Singularity container automatically, so you don't need to separately install each one's own dependencies.

Compute quality metrics and postprocessing outputs (waveforms, templates, ISI violation rates, and more) on each sorting result, then either curate manually (label units as good/noise/etc.) or apply an automatic curation rule based on the quality metrics, before exporting the curated result to Phy for final visual inspection.

If you're comparing multiple sorters or validating against ground truth, use the comparison module to directly benchmark one sorting output against another (or against known ground-truth spike times), producing standard agreement/precision/recall statistics.
tutorial_output: A curated Sorting object (spike times and cluster labels) per sorter run, exportable to Phy's native format for visualization, plus computed quality metrics and postprocessing outputs (waveforms, templates, correlograms) per unit — and, if multiple sorters were compared, agreement statistics quantifying how consistently different algorithms identified the same units.

sample_data.text: The paper's benchmark datasets are on the DANDI archive.

extra_links.label: spikeinterface-gui (Qt-based interactive viewer for sorting results)

title: Cellpose: a generalist algorithm for cellular segmentation
authors: Stringer C., Wang T., Michaelos M., Pachitariu M.
summary: Cellpose is a generalist deep-learning segmentation model that identifies cell and nucleus boundaries in a huge range of microscopy image types with no retraining or parameter adjustment, since its release evolved through human-in-the-loop fine-tuning (Cellpose 2.0), built-in image restoration (Cellpose3), and a foundation-model-scale generalist (Cellpose-SAM) — usable via GUI, Python API, or napari plugin.
abstract_long: Cellpose predicts a spatial flow field for every pixel toward its cell's center, then groups pixels by following these flows to their common source — a formulation that handles cells of highly varied shape and size better than direct boundary or mask prediction, and generalizes to 3D by combining flows computed from 2D slices along different axes without requiring 3D-labeled training data. The original model was trained on a dataset of over 70,000 segmented objects spanning many imaging modalities and cell types. Since publication, the tool has evolved substantially: Cellpose 2.0 added human-in-the-loop retraining (correct the model's mistakes on a few images, retrain in minutes, repeat) so users can quickly specialize the generalist model to their own data; Cellpose3 added one-click image restoration (denoising, deblurring, upsampling) integrated into the segmentation workflow; and the latest Cellpose-SAM model (built on a vision transformer) further improves generalization across contrast conditions, channel orderings, and object sizes.
data_acquisition: Any 2D or 3D microscopy image containing cells or nuclei (fluorescence, brightfield, phase contrast) — the model generalizes across imaging modalities without retraining
animal: Not applicable — general-purpose cell/nucleus segmentation, not species-specific (trained data includes tissue from mouse, among many other sources)
tutorial_intro: Cellpose works out of the box on a wide range of microscopy images via its pretrained generalist models — you typically don't need to train your own model unless the built-in models perform poorly on your specific data, in which case the human-in-the-loop workflow lets you fine-tune quickly.
tutorial_steps: Install with pip install cellpose[gui] (the [gui] extra adds the graphical interface; omit it if you only need the Python API/CLI). A GPU is recommended for speed but not required.

Try a pretrained model on your images first — either via the GUI (drag and drop an image, choose a model, click run) or the Python API: from cellpose import models; model = models.Cellpose(model_type='cyto3'); masks, flows, styles, diams = model.eval(image, diameter=None, channels=[0,0]), where cyto3 is the current super-generalist model and diameter=None lets Cellpose auto-estimate the typical cell size in your image.

If segmentation quality is poor on your specific data, use the human-in-the-loop workflow in the GUI: correct a handful of the model's mistakes by hand, retrain from those corrections in a few minutes, and re-run — repeating this cycle a few times typically gets you a model specialized to your data without needing hundreds of fully manual annotations.

If your images are noisy, blurry, or undersampled, try Cellpose3's built-in restoration models (denoising, deblurring, upsampling) before or as part of segmentation — accessible from the GUI or via the CellposeDenoiseModel class in the Python API.

For 3D volumes, pass your full 3D array and set do_3D=True in model.eval() — Cellpose computes 2D flows along each axis and combines them into a 3D flow field, so no 3D-labeled training data is needed.
tutorial_output: A labeled instance mask (each detected cell/nucleus assigned a unique integer ID, 0 for background) matching your input image dimensions, plus the underlying flow fields and per-cell diameter estimates — the mask can be exported for downstream quantification (cell counts, morphology, per-cell fluorescence intensity) or opened in the GUI/napari for visual inspection and correction.

extra_links.label: cellpose-napari (plugin for the napari image viewer)

title: A cell type-specific cortico-subcortical brain circuit for investigatory and novelty-seeking behavior
authors: Ahmadlou M., Houba J.H.W., van Vierbergen J.F.M., Giannouli M., Gimenez G.-A., van Weeghel C., Darbanfouladi M., Shirazi M.Y., Dziubek J., Kacem M., de Winter F., Heimel J.A.
summary: Using a 3-state hidden Markov model fit to JAABA-labeled investigatory action sequences, this paper distinguishes "deep" from "shallow" investigation of novel objects/conspecifics, and identifies a prelimbic-cortex-to-zona-incerta-to-periaqueductal-gray circuit — with a TAC1+ inhibitory zona incerta subpopulation in particular — that drives this novelty-seeking, curiosity-motivated behavior.
abstract_long: The authors found that inhibitory neurons in the medial zona incerta (ZIm), a subthalamic region, are essential for mice to initiate deep, sustained investigation of novel objects or conspecifics. ZIm neurons receive excitatory input from prelimbic cortex signaling the initiation of exploration, with the strength of this drive modulated by the animal's investigatory motivation. Behavior was labeled frame-by-frame with JAABA, then collapsed into a single ranked action per time step and fit with a 3-state hidden Markov model (idle, low-interest investigation, high-interest investigation) to characterize how action-sequence structure differs between novel and familiar objects/conspecifics. This let the authors define a continuous "depth of investigation" measure independent of raw interaction duration — for objects, whether a sniff is followed by a bite (deep) or not (shallow); for conspecifics, whether approach is followed by investigation with grabbing (deep) or without (shallow). Optogenetic activation of ZIm inhibitory neurons (particularly a TAC1-expressing subpopulation) increased positive arousal and investigatory depth by inhibiting the periaqueductal gray, establishing a prelimbic-cortex to ZIm to PAG circuit as a core substrate for curiosity-driven investigatory behavior.
data_acquisition: Mouse behavioral video (frame-by-frame labeled with JAABA) during object/conspecific investigation, combined with fiber photometry calcium recordings and optogenetic manipulation of zona incerta (ZIm) neurons
language: MATLAB (HMM fitting, behavior sequence analysis, photometry processing via InVivoTools); JAABA (Matlab/Java) for behavior labeling
animal: Mouse
tutorial_intro: The pipeline has three distinct stages that each rely on a different tool: JAABA for frame-by-frame behavior labeling (a general-purpose, separately maintained open-source tool — reusable on its own for any mouse behavior video), custom MATLAB code in this repo for the HMM-based action-sequence analysis specifically, and InVivoTools for the fiber-photometry/physiology signal processing. There's no single "install and run" entry point — treat the repo as the reference implementation of the HMM analysis, to adapt to your own JAABA-labeled behavior data.
tutorial_steps: Label your raw behavior videos frame-by-frame with JAABA. For object interaction, the relevant labeled behaviors were approach, sniff, carry, grab and bite; for social interaction, approach, investigation (body/facial/anogenital sniffing and grabbing), grab, avoid, defense, and the intruder's own approach/defense.

Import the JAABA labels into MATLAB and collapse them into one non-overlapping action per time step by ranking behaviors by investigatory importance and keeping only the highest-ranked action at each step. For object interaction the rank order (lowest to highest) was: non-investigatory, approach, sniff, carry, grab, bite. For social interaction: non-investigatory, intruder's approach, mouse's approach, investigation/grabbing (highest). Bite/grab were ranked highest because their transition probability from sniff/investigation differed most between novel and familiar conditions — this is the specific signal the model is built to detect.

Fit a 3-state hidden Markov model to each trial's action sequence using MATLAB's built-in hmmtrain (Baum-Welch parameter estimation) and hmmviterbi (most-likely state path decoding) functions. Initialize the transition matrix with equal probabilities across all transitions (since there's no prior expectation of state structure) and the emission matrix from the observed frequency of each labeled behavior. The 3 states the model recovers correspond to idle (no investigatory action), low-interest investigation, and high-interest investigation.

Use the fitted HMM's transition probabilities to classify each investigatory event as deep or shallow: for objects, an event starting with sniff is "deep" if continued by a bite, otherwise "shallow"; for social interaction, an event starting with approach is "deep" if continued by investigation-with-grab, otherwise "shallow." An event ends once no investigatory action has occurred for at least 100 ms.

For fiber photometry signal processing (thresholding, artifact rejection) and pupil diameter extraction used to relate ZIm activity and arousal to these behavioral classifications, see InVivoTools (linked above) — a general-purpose physiology toolbox from the same lab, not specific to this paper.
tutorial_output: Per-trial action sequences reduced to single ranked actions per time bin, a fitted 3-state HMM (transition and emission matrices) per condition (e.g. novel vs. familiar object/conspecific), and a deep-vs-shallow classification for every investigatory event — the behavioral measure that the paper then correlates with ZIm fiber-photometry activity and optogenetic manipulation effects.

sample_data.text: Processed data and analysis scripts are archived on Zenodo. Raw movies and additional scripts are on institutional storage, available from the authors on request.

extra_links.label: JAABA (frame-by-frame behavior labeling, used to generate the HMM's input sequences)
InVivoTools (fiber photometry and physiology signal processing, incl. pupil diameter extraction)

title: Anipose: A toolkit for robust markerless 3D pose estimation
authors: Karashchuk P., Rupp K.L., Dickinson E.S., Walling-Bell S., Sanders E., Azim E., Brunton B.W., Tuthill J.C.
summary: Anipose extends 2D markerless pose estimation (built on DeepLabCut) to robust 3D tracking from multiple synchronized cameras, adding automated camera calibration, 2D and 3D filters that remove tracking errors using the spatiotemporal structure of animal movement, and a web-based visualization tool — evaluated on flies, mice, and humans with sub-degree/sub-millimeter accuracy in most frames.
abstract_long: Anipose implements the full 3D tracking pipeline: (1) a robust camera calibration module that estimates each camera's parameters from videos of a moving calibration board via "iterative bundle adjustment" (a procedure that automatically down-weights outlier keypoint detections across several optimization stages); (2) 2D filters — a median filter, a Viterbi filter (finding the most temporally consistent path through each frame's top-N candidate keypoint detections), and a learned autoencoder filter (correcting confidence scores using correlations among joints) — that clean up per-camera 2D keypoint detections before triangulation; (3) a spatiotemporal 3D triangulation optimization that enforces smooth movement over time and constant limb length across frames, further reducing tracking errors and producing markedly smoother derivative (movement-speed) estimates than raw triangulation, RANSAC, or a simple 3D median filter; and (4) a structured project file format plus a web-based visualization tool for reviewing and annotating tracked videos at scale. Validated on a precision-manufactured calibration board (sub-20-micron length error, sub-1-degree angle error in over 90% of frames) and on walking Drosophila, reaching mice, and the Human 3.6M walking dataset, Anipose reveals that fly middle legs are driven primarily by femur rotation while front and hind legs are driven primarily by femur-tibia flexion — a finding invisible to 2D tracking alone.
data_acquisition: Synchronized multi-camera video (calibration board plus behavior videos), with 2D keypoints detected by an existing 2D pose-estimation network (DeepLabCut, or compatible tools like SLEAP/DeepPoseKit)
animal: Fruit fly (Drosophila), mouse, human; general-purpose across species
tutorial_intro: Anipose requires synchronized video from 3 or more cameras (2 can work for some setups, but 3+ evenly spaced around the animal is recommended so every joint is visible from at least 2 cameras at all times) — it does not do 2D tracking itself, relying on DeepLabCut (or, with a one-file change, SLEAP or DeepPoseKit) for that step. Users don't need to know Python: after initial setup, the pipeline runs from a configuration file and a small set of terminal commands.
tutorial_steps: Set up your multi-camera rig and record calibration videos: film a standard calibration board (a ChArUco board is recommended, since its keypoints remain detectable even with partial occlusion) moved by hand through all cameras' fields of view.

Organize your project using Anipose's standardized file structure (a specific folder layout for behavior videos, calibration videos, and configuration files), which lets project-wide commands operate on every video at once rather than one at a time.

Run anipose calibrate to estimate each camera's intrinsic and extrinsic parameters via iterative bundle adjustment — a good calibration should have an average reprojection error under 3 pixels (ideally under 1).
Detect 2D keypoints in your behavior videos with DeepLabCut (or a compatible 2D tracker), then run anipose analyze to process every video in the project.

Apply Anipose's default 2D filters (median, Viterbi, and/or autoencoder — configurable per dataset) to clean up the raw 2D detections, then run the 3D triangulation step with spatiotemporal regularization to obtain filtered, smooth 3D poses and joint angles.

Review results with the web-based visualization tool, which synchronously displays all camera views alongside the reconstructed 3D keypoints and lets you annotate behaviors directly on the tracked videos — useful for isolating specific behaviors (for example, labeling reach outcomes as hits, misses, or bumps) for downstream analysis.

If tracking quality is poor, start troubleshooting with the most common causes: insufficient or poorly distributed calibration board detections, too few cameras for the number of joints being tracked, or a 2D network that hasn't seen a particular pose before (in which case, identify and relabel outlier frames, then retrain).
tutorial_output: Per-frame 3D keypoint positions and joint angles for every tracked animal, plus camera calibration parameters (reusable across sessions with the same camera rig) and, where 3D filtering was applied, smoothed position and velocity trajectories suitable for direct kinematic analysis (for example, UMAP embedding of joint angles and their derivatives, as demonstrated in the paper for fly and human gait).

sample_data.text: Raw and analyzed data from all four evaluation datasets (ChArUco board, mouse reaching, fly walking, human walking) are on Dryad; the human dataset is the publicly available Human 3.6M dataset.

extra_links.label: aniposelib (standalone camera calibration and triangulation library, usable independently)
DeepLabCut (the 2D pose-estimation tool Anipose is built on)

title: SLEAP: A deep learning system for multi-animal pose tracking
authors: Pereira T.D., Tabris N., Matsliah A., Turner D.M., Li J., Ravindranath S., Papadoyannis E.S., Normand E., Deutsch D.S., Wang Z.Y., McKenzie-Smith G.C., Mitelut C.C., Diez Castro M., D'Uva J., Kislin M., Sanes D.H., Kocher S.D., Wang S.S.-H., Falkner A.L., Shaevitz J.W., Murthy M.
summary: SLEAP is a general-purpose deep learning framework for tracking the pose and identity of multiple interacting animals from video, offering both bottom-up and top-down pose-estimation strategies, two identity-tracking approaches (temporal and appearance-based), an accessible GUI requiring no coding, and real-time inference fast enough for closed-loop optogenetic experiments.
abstract_long: SLEAP (Social LEAP Estimates Animal Poses) is the multi-animal successor to LEAP, built as a complete, general-purpose pose-tracking system covering labeling, training, inference, and proofreading. It implements both bottom-up (detect all body parts, then group them into animals via part affinity fields) and top-down (detect each animal first, then find its body parts within a crop) strategies, over 30 configurable neural network architectures built around a modular UNet, and two identity-tracking approaches — temporal (optical-flow-based, propagating identities frame to frame) and appearance-based (classifying identity directly from learned visual features, immune to error propagation over long recordings). Evaluated across seven datasets spanning flies, bees, mice, and gerbils, SLEAP matches or exceeds prior single-animal tools in accuracy while running 2-5x faster, achieves 90% peak accuracy with as few as 200 labeled frames, and reaches inference speeds over 800 frames per second with latencies under 3.5 ms at full 1,024x1,024 resolution — fast enough that the authors demonstrate closed-loop optogenetic control of one fly's behavior triggered in real time by a detected social interaction with another fly.
data_acquisition: Video of one or more freely-moving or interacting animals of any species, from top-down or side camera angles
animal: Fruit flies, bumblebees, mice, gerbils (general-purpose, demonstrated across species)
tutorial_intro: SLEAP can be used entirely through its GUI with no programming required, or scripted via its Python API for custom pipelines and batch processing. It works on raw video or image arrays, and can also import existing annotations from other pose-tracking tools (DeepLabCut, DeepPoseKit) or standard formats (COCO).
tutorial_steps: Install SLEAP via pip or conda (conda distributions include automatic GPU support on Windows/Linux); it runs on Windows, Linux, or macOS with or without a GPU, though a GPU is strongly recommended for training and fast inference.

Label training data using SLEAP's GUI: define a skeleton (the set of body parts and their connections) appropriate for your animal, then annotate a representative set of frames — the paper found 90% peak accuracy achievable with as few as 200 labeled frames for both flies and mice.

Choose an approach and configure the model: bottom-up (single-pass, scales efficiently with many animals) or top-down (typically faster with few animals, but scales linearly with animal count); pick a network architecture (the default modular UNet, or one of 30+ alternatives with optional ImageNet-pretrained backbones for transfer learning) and receptive-field size via the GUI's configuration system, which serializes every setting to a reproducible JSON config.

Train the model from the GUI (which monitors loss curves and lets you issue manual early stopping) or via the CLI/API for remote/batch training — SLEAP can also train and run inference in a Google Colab notebook with GPU support after exporting a self-contained "training package" from your local installation.

If you need to track identity across frames, choose between the two tracking modes: flow-shift (temporal, optical-flow-based, needs no extra labeling but can propagate rare ID-switch errors over time) or an appearance-based ID model (requires labeling each training instance with its identity class, but eliminates error propagation — recommended for long recordings or animals with subtle but consistent individual differences, such as the gerbil dataset in the paper).

Run inference on new video via the CLI, high-level Python API, or GUI; results (including confidence-scored predictions) can be reopened in the GUI for proofreading, and raw positional data can be exported in formats convenient for downstream analysis or for use with other tools such as SimBA or B-SOiD.
tutorial_output: Per-frame, per-animal body-part coordinates with confidence scores, plus (if tracking is enabled) a consistent identity/track assignment across frames — exportable as SLEAP's own portable file format (which can include the source images) or as raw positional arrays for downstream analysis in your own pipeline or in third-party behavior-classification tools.

sample_data.text: All seven benchmark datasets (7,636 labeled images, 15,441 animal instances across flies, bees, mice, and gerbils) plus over 300 trained models (~90 GB) are publicly archived.

extra_links.label: Conda packages for core dependencies (TensorFlow, NumPy, OpenCV, PySide2)

title: Learnable latent embeddings for joint behavioural and neural analysis
authors: Schneider S., Lee J.H., Mathis M.W.
summary: CEBRA is a contrastive-learning method that jointly embeds neural activity and behavioral data (or neural data alone, self-supervised) into a low-dimensional, consistent latent space, improving decoding accuracy over standard supervised approaches and letting you compare embeddings across sessions, subjects, and even recording modalities (for example, two-photon calcium imaging versus Neuropixels).
abstract_long: CEBRA (Consistent EmBeddings of high-dimensional Recordings using Auxiliary variables) combines ideas from nonlinear ICA with contrastive learning to produce latent embeddings of neural time series conditioned on behavior and/or time. It supports three modes: fully supervised/hypothesis-driven (using behavioral labels to shape the embedding), self-supervised/discovery-driven (using only time, with no labels required), and hybrid. Unlike many representation-learning approaches, CEBRA doesn't rely on data augmentation or a specific generative model, and it can jointly train across multiple sessions, subjects, and even recording modalities, producing embeddings that are directly comparable across them. The authors validate CEBRA on calcium imaging and electrophysiology datasets spanning sensory, motor, and memory systems in mice, macaques, and flies — including decoding hippocampal position, uncovering kinematic features from motor cortex, and producing consistent embeddings that let two-photon and Neuropixels recordings of the same brain area be compared directly.
data_acquisition: Not applicable — a general-purpose representation-learning method for time-series neural data (validated on both calcium imaging and electrophysiology) paired with behavioral labels
animal: Not applicable — demonstrated across species and recording modalities (mouse, macaque, fly)
tutorial_intro: CEBRA expects neural activity (spike counts, calcium traces, or any other time-series neural signal) as a 2D array (timepoints x features/neurons), optionally paired with a behavioral variable of the same length if you want to use the supervised/hypothesis-driven mode.
tutorial_steps: Install with pip install cebra (GPU with PyTorch/CUDA recommended for anything beyond quick tests).

Instantiate a model: from cebra import CEBRA; cebra_model = CEBRA(model_architecture='offset10-model', batch_size=512, max_iterations=10000, output_dimension=8) — key choices are the model architecture, the output embedding dimensionality, and (for supervised mode) which behavioral variables to condition on.

Fit the model to your data: cebra_model.fit(neural_data) for self-supervised/discovery-driven embeddings (time-only), or cebra_model.fit(neural_data, behavior_labels) to additionally condition on a behavioral variable (hypothesis-driven) — you can pass either continuous or discrete labels, and multiple label arrays for a hybrid approach.

Generate the embedding: embedding = cebra_model.transform(neural_data) gives you the low-dimensional latent representation, which you can then use for decoding (for example, fitting a simple classifier/regressor from embedding to behavior), visualization, or comparing consistency across sessions/subjects/modalities.

To compare embeddings across multiple sessions or animals (a key use case in the paper), fit CEBRA jointly across datasets and use the built-in consistency metrics to quantify how similar the resulting embeddings are — low consistency can itself be a meaningful finding about differences between sessions or subjects, not just a nuisance to eliminate.
tutorial_output: A low-dimensional embedding (an array of shape timepoints x output_dimension) representing your neural data in a space shaped by whichever behavioral variables (if any) you conditioned on — used downstream for decoding accuracy benchmarks, visualization of neural manifolds, or quantifying representational consistency across recording sessions, animals, or modalities.

sample_data.text: The repo's demo notebooks include example neural and behavioral datasets (hippocampus position-decoding and other benchmarks) to run the full pipeline without your own data.

title: AlphaTracker: a multi-animal tracking and behavioral analysis tool
authors: Chen Z., Zhang R., Fang H.-S., Zhang Y.E., Bal A., Zhou H., Rock R.R., Padilla-Coreano N., Keyes L.R., Zhu H., Li Y.-L., Komiyama T., Tye K.M., Lu C.
summary: AlphaTracker is a markerless multi-animal pose-tracking and behavioral-clustering pipeline (built on AlphaPose/YOLOv3) with a GUI or command-line workflow that outperforms SLEAP and DeepLabCut on identity tracking of near-identical mice, plus an unsupervised hierarchical-clustering module for discovering individual and social behavioral motifs from the tracked poses.
abstract_long: AlphaTracker's tracking pipeline has three steps: YOLOv3 detects each animal's bounding box, a Squeeze-and-Excitation Network (SENet) estimates keypoints within each box, and a custom identity-tracking method (comparing hierarchical position/orientation descriptors via intersection-over-union, refined with Kalman filtering) maintains consistent animal identities across frames — important because same-strain animals look nearly identical. On benchmark datasets (two mice in a home cage; four mice in an operant chamber), AlphaTracker outperformed both DeepLabCut and SLEAP on keypoint accuracy (mAP) and tracking consistency (MOTA/MOTP), including with as few as 50 training frames. A separate behavioral-clustering module groups 15-frame (500 ms) pose clips via agglomerative hierarchical clustering into individual behaviors (walking, digging, sniffing, rearing, turning, grooming) and, for interacting dyads, social behaviors (following, chasing, anogenital/face sniffing, social rearing) — validated against human annotation with an Adjusted Rand Index well above chance. Everything is usable via a code-free GUI or the command line, with a Google Colab option for users without local GPU access.
data_acquisition: Standard top-down video of multiple unmarked animals — works with low-cost webcams (tested down to 540p), no specialized hardware or markers required
animal: Mouse (demonstrated); adaptable to other species with retraining on new annotated data
tutorial_intro: AlphaTracker offers both a code-free GUI and a command-line workflow; either way it expects either your own annotated training frames (to train a custom model) or just a raw video (to use the bundled pretrained demo model). Windows users should check out the repo's "windows" branch before installing, since the default build relies on a Linux-only C-based YOLO toolbox.
tutorial_steps: Install: git clone https://github.com/MVIG-SJTU/AlphaTracker.git, then cd AlphaTracker and bash scripts/install.sh (Windows users first run git checkout windows). This sets up an Anaconda environment with all dependencies. Alternatively, skip local installation entirely using the Colab notebooks linked above.

(Optional — skip if using the bundled pretrained demo model) Annotate your own training frames with the included Sloth-based annotation tool under ./Tracking/TheAnnotationTool/: draw a bounding box plus your chosen keypoints (the paper used snout, left ear, right ear, tail base) for at least ~200 representative frames, keeping the same labeling order for every animal in every frame.

Train the tracking model, either via the GUI's "Train" button or by setting paths and parameters (image/annotation folders, number of animals, number of keypoints) in ./Tracking/AlphaTracker/setting.py and running python train.py. In the paper, 600 annotated frames were enough to outperform DeepLabCut and SLEAP on identity-tracking accuracy; even 50 frames reached an mAP above 0.7.

Run tracking on a new video via the GUI or python track.py, after setting the video path, frame range, and expected number of animals in setting.py — or set exp_name=demo to use the bundled pretrained model without training your own.

Inspect and correct tracking errors with the browser-based curation UI (python setup.py inside the UI/ folder). Large jitter in the keypoint timeline usually means the pose model needs more training data; individual misidentified animals or mislabeled keypoints can be corrected frame-by-frame.

Run behavioral clustering on the tracked poses with python fft_main_sep_twoMiceInteract.py, after configuring feature weights in ./BehavioralClustering/setting.py (set social-feature weights to 0 if you only want individual-behavior clustering). This groups 15-frame (500 ms) pose clips — matching the sub-second timescale of mouse behavior — via agglomerative hierarchical clustering.

Inspect clustering quality with the provided Jupyter notebook (dendrograms, feature heatmaps, UMAP, mutual-information plots) to choose a good distance threshold, then review, merge, or rename clusters in the browser-based clustering UI.
tutorial_output: Per-frame keypoint coordinates and consistent animal identities for every tracked animal (exportable as JSON), plus — from the clustering step — a set of individual behavior clusters (walking, digging, sniffing, rearing, grooming, etc.) and, for multi-animal videos, social behavior clusters (following, chasing, anogenital/face sniffing, social rearing), each represented by a characteristic average pose trajectory.

sample_data.text: A demo training dataset (600 annotated frames of two unmarked mice interacting in a home cage) and a bundled demo video are provided for a quick first run.

Quick-test Colab notebook (pretrained model, no local install)
Training Colab notebook (train on your own annotated data)

title: Bayesian multilevel hidden Markov models identify stable state dynamics in longitudinal recordings from macaque primary motor cortex
authors: Kirchherr S., Mildiner Moraga S., Coudé G., Bimbi M., Ferrari P.F., Aarts E., Bonaiuto J.J.
summary: This paper introduces a multilevel Bayesian hidden Markov model (mHMMbayes) for longitudinal multi-electrode spiking data, using a multivariate Poisson log-normal emission distribution and trial-specific random effects so that hidden neural population states — and their relationship to behavior — generalize consistently across multiple days of recording, unlike a standard single-level HMM which failed to generalize across sessions in the same dataset.
abstract_long: Chronically implanted multi-electrode arrays let researchers record from the same neural population over weeks or months, but standard hidden Markov model (HMM) approaches to segmenting this activity into discrete population states assume the same transition and emission parameters apply to every trial — ignoring the nested, trial-by-trial and day-by-day structure of longitudinal recordings. The authors' multilevel Bayesian HMM instead estimates trial-specific transition and emission parameters (centered around group-level means) via a multivariate Poisson log-normal emission distribution suited to multi-electrode spike-count data, fit with an iterative Bayesian (Gibbs-based) estimation procedure rather than classic expectation-maximization. Applied to macaque primary motor cortex activity recorded across 10 days during a reaching-grasping-placing task, the model identified five-to-six discrete population states whose onset/offset times were tightly and stably linked to behavioral events (movement onset, object contact, placing) across the entire recording period — a relationship a comparison single-level HMM could not reliably recover, since it lacks trial-specific parameters and so cannot generalize the same state definitions across sessions recorded on different days.
data_acquisition: Multi-unit spiking activity from chronically implanted multi-electrode arrays (macaque primary motor cortex), recorded across multiple days during a reaching, grasping, and placing task
animal: Macaque (Macaca mulatta)
tutorial_intro: mHMMbayes expects binned spike counts (the paper used 10 ms bins) per electrode, per trial, optionally alongside trial-level covariates (such as experimental condition) that you want the transition probabilities to depend on. It's not yet on CRAN — the multilevel Poisson log-normal functionality used in this paper lives on the package's "develop" branch.
tutorial_steps: Install the development version directly from GitHub, e.g. remotes::install_github("smildiner/mHMMbayes", ref = "develop"), to get the HMM_plnorm (single-level) and mHMM_plnorm (multilevel) functions used in this paper.
Prepare your data as binned spike counts per electrode and trial, plus any trial-level covariates you want to include in the transition model.

Fit the model, specifying the number of hidden states, starting values for the group-level transition and emission parameters (a conventional EM-fit single-level HMM — for example via the depmixS4 package — is a convenient source for these starting values), and non-informative hyper-priors for the group-level parameters.

Select the number of states by comparing relative fit (AIC/BIC) across several candidate values, and confirm convergence of all group-level parameters using the multivariate potential scale reduction factor (target Ȓ below 1.05) across at least two additional chains with randomized starting values.

Validate the fitted model with Bayesian posterior predictive checks: simulate new datasets from the fitted model and compare summary statistics (mean, standard deviation, maximum counts, proportion of zeros) against your real data, aggregated across trials per electrode.

Decode the most likely hidden-state sequence for each trial using the Viterbi algorithm with that trial's own estimated trial-specific parameters — this trial-specific decoding (rather than one shared parameter set for every trial) is the paper's key advantage over a standard single-level HMM for longitudinal data.

Relate the decoded state onset/offset times and state statistics (number of activations per trial, state lifetime) to your own behavioral event timings using your own correlation or regression approach — the package provides the fitted states and their forward probabilities, and downstream behavioral analysis is left to the user (the paper's own such analysis code is a separate repository — see the link above).
tutorial_output: A fitted multilevel HMM with group-level and trial-specific estimates of the transition probability matrix and the Poisson log-normal emission means per electrode and state (each with credibility intervals), plus, via the Viterbi algorithm, a decoded most-likely hidden-state sequence for every trial — from which state onset/offset times, activation counts, and lifetimes can be computed and related to behavioral events or experimental conditions.

sample_data.text: The macaque M1 spiking dataset analyzed in the paper is openly available on Zenodo.

title: SaLSa: A Combinatory Approach of Semi-Automatic Labeling and Long Short-Term Memory to Classify Behavioral Syllables
authors: Sakata S.
summary: SaLSa combines a semi-automatic labeling pipeline (unsupervised PCA/UMAP/spectral clustering to surface behavioral-syllable candidates for fast manual labeling) with an LSTM classifier trained on the resulting labels, reaching over 97% classification accuracy for six mouse behavioral syllables (locomotion, turning, rearing, sniffing, grooming, pause) from DeepLabCut-tracked open-field video — used to show that female 5xFAD Alzheimer's-model mice specifically develop hyperlocomotion between 4 and 8 months of age.
abstract_long: LSTM networks are well suited to behavioral syllable classification because behavior often has long-term temporal dependencies that convolutional or frame-by-frame approaches don't capture — but LSTMs need substantial labeled training data. SaLSa addresses this with a two-stage pipeline: first, semi-automatic labeling, where 910 spatial and temporal features (extracted from egocentric, DeepLabCut-tracked body-part coordinates via PCA dimensionality reduction, UMAP embedding, and deliberately over-split spectral clustering) surface candidate behavioral-syllable snippets that a human then labels quickly via a GUI, rather than labeling raw video from scratch; second, an LSTM classifier (a 200-unit LSTM layer plus fully connected/softmax/classification layers) trained on those labels. Evaluated on independently labeled videos, the trained classifier reached over 97% accuracy and AUC above 0.95 for most syllables (locomotion, turning, rearing, grooming, pause; sniffing was harder to classify reliably). Benchmarked against keypoint-MoSeq — a leading fully-unsupervised alternative — SaLSa's top-down, predefined-syllable approach classified grooming reliably where keypoint-MoSeq tended to misclassify it, though keypoint-MoSeq automatically subdivided syllables like locomotion and turning by movement direction that SaLSa does not distinguish. Applying the trained classifier across 43 mice, the author found that female 5xFAD mice develop significantly elevated locomotion specifically between 4 and 8 months old, while age-related decline in rearing was common to both sexes and genotypes.
data_acquisition: Top-down webcam video (25 fps) of a single mouse in an open-field arena, pose-tracked with DeepLabCut
animal: Mouse (5xFAD Alzheimer's-disease model and wild-type littermates)
tutorial_intro: SaLSa expects DeepLabCut-tracked body-part coordinates from top-down open-field video as its starting point — the paper tracked 10 points (nose, head, left/right ear, neck, anterior/posterior back, tail base, mid-tail, tail tip), though the two tail points were later excluded since tail shape didn't reflect behavioral syllables in this setup. All downstream feature extraction, labeling, and classification are implemented as MATLAB scripts. Note: independent peer review of this paper found the package's usability had some rough edges (e.g. no early-stopping during LSTM training, no dataloader for large files) — budget some troubleshooting time if you're setting this up for the first time.
tutorial_steps: Track your mouse video with DeepLabCut, labeling at minimum nose, head, ears, neck, and back/tail-base body parts.

Convert tracked coordinates to egocentric coordinates (in the paper, the neck was set as the body center and the nose-neck axis as the body-center axis), then extract SaLSa's feature set: spatial features (relative coordinates across body parts, relative angle of each body part to the body-center axis, inter-body-part distances) and temporal features (frame-by-frame velocities of positions and distances, plus their spectrotemporal characteristics via wavelet transform using MATLAB's cwt function) — 910 features total in the paper's configuration, which assumes a fixed frame rate (25 fps); a different frame rate changes the feature count and requires retraining.

Run the unsupervised syllable-candidate identification: PCA to reduce dimensionality (keep enough components to explain over 85% variance — around 15 components in the paper), UMAP for further reduction to 2D (paper used min_dist=0.3, n_neighbors=5), then spectral clustering into a deliberately large number of clusters (35-50, chosen via the Calinski-Harabasz criterion) so each cluster stays relatively free of contamination from other behaviors. Discard fragmented sequences under 0.25 s, since they're too short to label reliably.

Manually label each remaining cluster snippet using SaLSa's built-in GUI, assigning it to one of your predefined behavioral syllables (the paper used locomotion, turning, rearing, sniffing, grooming, pause, plus a miscellaneous catch-all for contaminated or unrecognized snippets) — this semi-automatic step is much faster than labeling video from scratch, since the unsupervised step has already surfaced syllable-like candidates for you to confirm or reject.
