Train the LSTM classifier on your labeled data: an input layer sized to your feature count, an LSTM layer (200 hidden units in the paper), a fully connected layer, a softmax layer, and a classification layer — trained with the ADAM optimizer and L2 regularization (paper defaults: gradient threshold 1, up to 60 epochs, 80/20 train/validation split), keeping the model with the best validation performance.

Evaluate on independently labeled videos not used in training, computing an ROC curve and AUC per behavioral syllable, before trusting the classifier on new, unlabeled data — in the paper, most syllables reached AUC above 0.95, but rarer syllables (sniffing, at under 1% of labeled frames) classified less reliably and were excluded from downstream analysis.

Run the trained classifier on your full video set to get frame-by-frame syllable labels, then compute per-episode metrics — speed (nose travel distance per frame), cumulative turning angle (of the nose-to-tail-base axis), and "compactness" (mean pairwise body-part distance) — to characterize each syllable quantitatively or compare syllable fractions and durations across experimental groups.
tutorial_output: Frame-by-frame behavioral syllable labels for every processed video, per-syllable ROC/AUC performance metrics when evaluated against held-out labeled data, and derived per-episode kinematic summaries (speed, turning angle, compactness) usable for downstream group comparisons such as genotype, sex, or age effects on syllable usage.

extra_links.label: DeepLabCut (the pose-estimation tool SaLSa's tracking step depends on)

title: SpatialData: an open and universal data framework for spatial omics
authors: Marconato L., Palla G., Yamauchi K.A., Virshup I., Heidari E., Treis T., Vierdag W.-M., Toth M., Stockhaus S., Shrestha R.B., Rombaut B., Pollaris L., Lehner L., Vöhringer H., Kats I., Saeys Y., Saka S.K., Huber W., Gerstung M., Moore J., Theis F.J., Stegle O.
summary: SpatialData is a Python framework and file format (built on Zarr/OME-NGFF) for storing, aligning, querying, and jointly analyzing spatial omics datasets across technologies (Xenium, Visium, MERFISH, CosMx, MIBI-TOF, imaging mass cytometry, CyCIF), letting you register multiple modalities to a common coordinate system and aggregate data across them for integrative analysis.
abstract_long: SpatialData represents any spatial omics dataset using five primitive elements — Images, Labels (segmentation masks), Points (molecule detections), Shapes (regions/capture locations), and Tables (quantifications/annotations) — serialized to a technology-agnostic Zarr store built on the OME-NGFF specification, so data from different platforms and vendors share one programmatic interface. The Python library supports lazy loading of larger-than-memory datasets, coordinate transformations for aligning multiple datasets to a common coordinate system, and query/aggregation operators for transferring annotations (cell types, regions of interest, gene expression) across modalities and spatial scales. The authors demonstrate this on a breast cancer study combining Xenium (in situ sequencing) and Visium (spot-based) data: aligning replicate slides via interactively-selected landmarks, transferring histology-derived regions of interest and copy-number-based clonal annotations across datasets, and comparing cell-type-fraction estimates from Xenium counts versus Visium deconvolution (cell2location). SpatialData interoperates with the broader scverse ecosystem (Scanpy, Squidpy, scvi-tools) and provides a PyTorch Dataset class for training deep learning models directly from spatial data tiles.
data_acquisition: Not applicable — a general-purpose data framework compatible with all major spatial omics technologies (imaging-based and sequencing-based), not tied to one acquisition modality
animal: Not applicable — works on human or any species' spatial omics data
tutorial_intro: SpatialData is a general-purpose framework rather than a single-analysis tool — it standardizes how you load, align, and query spatial omics data, and you then plug in your preferred downstream analysis packages (Scanpy, Squidpy, cell2location, etc.). It's a pure Python package (3.9+), installable via pip, with satellite packages for visualization (napari-spatialdata), format-specific readers (spatialdata-io), and static plotting (spatialdata-plot).
tutorial_steps: Install with pip (the core spatialdata package plus whichever satellite packages you need: napari-spatialdata for interactive viewing/annotation, spatialdata-io for vendor-format readers, spatialdata-plot for static figures).

Load your data using the appropriate spatialdata-io reader for your technology (for example, the 10x Xenium or Visium readers) — this parses vendor-specific output into the five standard SpatialData element types (Images, Labels, Points, Shapes, Tables) automatically.

If you have multiple datasets to integrate (for example, replicate sections or paired modalities), use napari-spatialdata to interactively select corresponding landmark points across images, then align them into a shared common coordinate system with SpatialData's landmark-based alignment function — this is what makes cross-modality queries and aggregation possible afterward.

Use SpatialData's query interface to extract a specific spatial region (as a bounding box or arbitrary polygon) across all aligned modalities at once, and its aggregation interface (aggregate, with fractions=True for compositional fractions) to transfer quantifications — such as summing molecule counts, or computing cell-type fractions — from one modality's elements (for example, individual Xenium cells) into another's (for example, Visium capture-location circles).

For downstream analysis, hand off the resulting SpatialData object (or its component AnnData tables) to standard scverse tools — Scanpy for expression analysis, Squidpy for spatial statistics, or cell2location for deconvolution — since SpatialData is designed to interoperate with these rather than replace them.

If you're training a deep learning model on spatial data, use SpatialData's built-in PyTorch Dataset class to generate training tiles (for example, image patches centered on cells) directly from a SpatialData object, avoiding a separate data-export step.
tutorial_output: A SpatialData object (backed by a single Zarr store on disk) containing your aligned, queryable multi-modal dataset — from this you extract whatever your downstream analysis needs: aligned images, per-cell or per-region gene expression tables, transferred annotations (cell types, ROIs, clonal labels) across modalities, or ready-to-train PyTorch tile datasets.

sample_data.text: More than 40 example datasets across 8 spatial omics technologies (CosMx, Xenium, Visium, CyCIF, MERFISH, MIBI-TOF, imaging mass cytometry) are provided pre-converted to the SpatialData format, downloadable in full or accessible directly from cloud (S3) storage.

title: Spike sorting with Kilosort4
authors: Pachitariu M., Sridhar S., Pennington J., Stringer C.
summary: Kilosort4 is a spike-sorting algorithm that extracts single-neuron firing times from extracellular electrophysiology recordings, introducing a graph-based clustering approach (built around modularity optimization and a hierarchical merging tree) that outperformed all prior algorithms — including earlier Kilosort versions — across a range of realistic drift simulations.
abstract_long: Spike sorting must contend with two hard problems: nonstationary spike waveforms (caused mainly by probe drift) and overlapping electrical fields between nearby neurons. Kilosort4 keeps the "template deconvolution" approach from earlier Kilosort versions (detecting spikes, including overlapping ones, via iterative matching pursuit against learned waveform templates, then extracting background-corrected spike features), but replaces the final clustering step with a new graph-based algorithm: an iterative neighbor-reassignment procedure (based on modularity optimization) that intentionally oversplits data into many small clusters, followed by a hierarchical "merging tree" that uses two criteria long favored by human curators — bimodality of the spike-projection distribution, and refractoriness of the cross-correlogram — to decide which clusters should be merged back together. To benchmark performance, the authors built realistic simulations using densely sampled electrical fields and drift patterns drawn from real Neuropixels recordings (including the International Brain Laboratory's public dataset). Kilosort4 outperformed all other tested algorithms (including SpyKING CIRCUS, MountainSort4, IronClust, and earlier Kilosort versions) across every drift condition tested, correctly identifying 80-90% of ground-truth units even under high drift, without an increase in false positives.
data_acquisition: Extracellular electrophysiology recordings from high-density probes (Neuropixels 1.0/2.0 and similar), stored as raw binary data
animal: Not applicable — general-purpose spike-sorting algorithm, validated on mouse Neuropixels recordings from the International Brain Laboratory (IBL)
tutorial_intro: Kilosort4 expects a flat binary data file (default int16) as input. If your recording is in a different format (NWB, Open Ephys, Blackrock, Neuralynx, Intan, etc.), convert it first using SpikeInterface (preferred, for compatibility with the downstream curation tool Phy) or use Kilosort's own SpikeInterface wrapper to load it without a separate conversion step.
tutorial_steps: Install Kilosort4 (a Python/PyTorch package) — GPU strongly recommended for anything beyond small test recordings, though PyTorch's CPU backend works for testing.

Set up your run via the GUI (built with pyqtgraph, replicating the earlier MATLAB GUI) or the Python API: point it at your binary data file, specify or construct a probe/channel-map configuration, and set the key parameters. The GUI displays a short data segment up front, which is the fastest way to catch configuration mistakes (misconfigured channel count shows as diagonal "streaking"; wrong channel order shows single-channel but no multi-channel waveforms).

Preprocessing runs automatically in this order: common average referencing, temporal high-pass filtering (300 Hz default), channel whitening (in local neighborhoods of ~32 channels), and drift correction — all computed on demand per data batch rather than as a separate precomputation pass, unlike earlier Kilosort versions.

The core algorithm then runs template deconvolution (detecting spikes, including overlapping ones, via matching pursuit against learned waveform templates) followed by graph-based clustering (oversplitting via iterative modularity-based reassignment, then merging via the hierarchical merging tree using bimodality and refractory-period criteria) — this all runs without manual intervention, though default parameters can be adjusted for probes with unusual geometry (tetrodes, single electrodes, ultra-dense arrays) or very long/chronic recordings.

Review and curate the output in Phy, the companion visualization tool that all Kilosort versions are designed to export to — even with Kilosort4's substantially reduced need for manual curation compared to earlier versions, the authors recommend continuing to check output quality there.
tutorial_output: A set of ".npy" files describing every detected unit — spike times, cluster assignments, and waveform templates — directly loadable in Phy for visualization and manual curation, plus diagnostic plots (drift traces, spike-rate summaries) generated during the run to help assess recording and sorting quality.

sample_data.text: All benchmark simulations draw drift patterns and waveforms from more than 500 publicly available Neuropixels recordings from the International Brain Laboratory (IBL).

title: Simple Behavioral Analysis (SimBA) as a platform for explainable machine learning in behavioral neuroscience
authors: Goodwin N.L., Choong J.J., Hwang S., Pitts K., Bloom L., Islam A., Zhang Y.Y., Szelenyi E.R., Tong X., Newman E.L., Miczek K., Wright H.R., McLaughlin R.J., Norville Z.C., Eshel N., Heshmati M., Nilsson S.R.O., Golden S.A.
summary: SimBA is a GUI-driven, open-source platform that turns pose-tracking data from any pose-estimation tool (DeepLabCut, SLEAP, etc.) into supervised random-forest behavioral classifiers, and — distinctively — builds in SHAP-based explainability so classifiers can be objectively compared and shared across labs, species, and pose-estimation schemes like a reusable research reagent.
abstract_long: SimBA sits downstream of pose estimation: after tracking animals with an external tool, users import the tracking data (CSV, H5, SLP, JSON, TRK, or MAT) and SimBA computes hundreds of per-frame features (movements, angles, paths, velocities, distances, sizes) across static and dynamic time windows, which are then used to train per-behavior random forest classifiers via an in-app annotation interface (manual, machine-assisted, or imported from BORIS/Noldus/EthoVisionXT). The platform's key innovation is built-in SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanation) analysis, letting researchers see which features and timescales drive each classification — and, because SHAP values can be grouped into ethologically defined feature categories, classifiers trained on different pose-estimation schemes (e.g. 5 vs. 8 tracked body parts) can still be directly compared. The authors demonstrate this by comparing independently built mouse and rat attack classifiers from six research sites, finding both high cross-site accuracy and SHAP-revealed differences in which features and timescales different annotators relied on — and use SHAP-quantified behavior to reveal sex and environment-dependent differences in aggression and coping behaviors during resident-intruder and chronic social defeat stress assays.
data_acquisition: Pose-tracking data imported from an existing markerless pose-estimation tool (DeepLabCut, SLEAP, DeepPoseKit, or MARS) — species-agnostic, validated on fish, wasp, moth, mouse, rat, and bird
animal: Species-agnostic; validated on fish, wasp, moth, mouse, rat, bird
tutorial_intro: SimBA does not perform pose estimation itself — you first track your animals with an external tool (DeepLabCut, SLEAP, DeepPoseKit, or MARS), then import that tracking data into SimBA for feature calculation, classifier training, and analysis.
tutorial_steps: Install with pip install Simba-UW-tf-dev (or via conda; see the docs for full environment setup).
(Optional) Pre-process raw videos within SimBA's batch tools: cropping, trimming, downsampling, or adjusting contrast/resolution before pose estimation.
Track your animals with your pose-estimation tool of choice (DeepLabCut, SLEAP, DeepPoseKit, or MARS), then import the resulting tracking files into a SimBA project via the GUI.

Apply SimBA's outlier-correction options if needed (movement and location criteria that flag and correct implausible frame-to-frame body-part jumps), then let SimBA calculate its default battery of features (movements, angles, paths, velocities, distances, sizes) across both single frames and rolling time windows — advanced users can define fully custom feature-extraction classes.

Build a training set for each behavior of interest: annotate frames directly in SimBA's built-in scoring interface (from raw video, or machine-assisted where you verify a prior model's predictions), or import existing annotations from BORIS, Noldus Observer, or EthoVisionXT. SimBA's video batch tools can extract targeted clips around the behavior of interest to balance positive/negative frames without requiring every frame of every video to be labeled.

Train a random forest classifier per behavior (SimBA's defaults: entropy criterion, sqrt max features, minimum sample leaf 1, 2,000 estimators — adjustable, with recommended settings importable from classifiers of similar behaviors). Evaluate with F1 learning curves and precision-recall curves, and use the interactive discrimination-threshold tool to set an appropriate probability cutoff for calling a behavior "present" in new videos.

Run the trained classifier on new videos, then use SimBA's built-in analysis tools (Gantt plots, probability plots, heatmaps, ROI-based time analyses) to extract behavior metrics — total duration, bout count, mean bout duration, and mean bout interval — with a Kleinberg-filter option to smooth frame-by-frame predictions into coherent temporal "bursts."

For explainability, compute SHAP values for your classifier (built on TreeSHAP) to see which features and timescales drive its predictions — group individual features into the ethologically defined categories described in the paper (or your own custom bins) to make classifiers built on different pose-estimation schemes or from different labs directly comparable.
tutorial_output: Per-frame behavior probabilities and binary classifications for every video analyzed, bout-level summary statistics (total duration, number of bouts, mean bout duration and interval) per behavior, visualizations (Gantt charts, probability traces, heatmaps, annotated video overlays) for qualitative validation, and — where computed — per-feature-category SHAP explainability scores that quantify and make comparable what each classifier is actually keying on.

title: Keypoint-MoSeq: parsing behavior by linking point tracking to pose dynamics
authors: Weinreb C., Pearl J.E., Lin S., Osman M.A.M., Zhang L., Annapragada S., Conlin E., Hoffmann R., Makowska S., Gillis W.F., Jay M., Ye S., Mathis A., Mathis M.W., Pereira T., Linderman S.W., Datta S.R.
summary: Keypoint-MoSeq is an unsupervised behavior-segmentation algorithm that fits a switching linear dynamical system to keypoint tracking data (from SLEAP, DeepLabCut, etc.), simultaneously denoising keypoint jitter and identifying discrete behavioral "syllables," outperforming prior clustering methods (B-SOiD, VAME, MotionMapper) at capturing true behavioral transitions across mice, rats and flies.
abstract_long: Traditional MoSeq requires 3D depth video and fails when applied directly to 2D/3D keypoint data, because high-frequency tracking jitter gets mistaken for behavioral transitions. The authors rebuilt MoSeq as a switching linear dynamical system (keypoint-MoSeq) with three hierarchical levels — a discrete syllable sequence, a low-dimensional pose trajectory, and per-keypoint noise estimates — so the model can attribute an implausible single-keypoint jump to noise while preserving a smooth underlying pose trajectory. Validated against accelerometry, striatal dopamine photometry, and expert behavior labels, keypoint-MoSeq produces syllables (median duration ~400 ms) that align far better with true behavioral transitions than B-SOiD, VAME, or MotionMapper, and generalizes across species (mice, rats, fruit flies) and timescales (from ~35 ms sniff-aligned head movements to multi-second syllables). Note: the code is free for academic and non-commercial research use under a Harvard University license (see the repo's LICENSE) — not a standard permissive open-source license, so commercial use requires separate arrangement.
data_acquisition: 2D or 3D keypoint tracking data from an existing pose-estimation pipeline (SLEAP, DeepLabCut, anipose, etc.), optionally paired with depth video, accelerometry or neural recordings for validation
animal: Mouse, rat, fruit fly (Drosophila) — demonstrated to generalize across species
tutorial_intro: Keypoint-MoSeq takes keypoint tracking data you've already generated with a separate pose-estimation tool — it doesn't do the initial tracking itself. It loads directly from several common formats (SLEAP, DeepLabCut, anipose, sleap-anipose, or NWB). A GPU is strongly recommended given its JAX backend; see the docs for exact installation and CUDA setup, which is OS/driver-dependent.
tutorial_steps: Load your keypoints with kpms.load_keypoints(keypoint_data_path, format), where format is one of 'sleap', 'deeplabcut', 'anipose', 'sleap-anipose', or 'nwb'.

Configure two key hyperparameters in the project config: latent_dimension (a good heuristic is the number of PCs needed to explain 90% of variance, or 10 — whichever is lower) and kappa (the "stickiness" hyperparameter that sets the target syllable timescale — higher values give longer, coarser syllables; lower values give shorter, finer-grained ones).

Fitting happens in two phases: first an AR-HMM is fit to a fixed pose trajectory derived from PCA of egocentrically-aligned keypoints (this is what the paper calls "MoSeq applied to keypoints," useful as a diagnostic baseline), then the full keypoint-MoSeq model is initialized from that AR-HMM and fit via Gibbs sampling — around 500 iterations, which took 30-60 minutes on a consumer GPU for about 5 hours of data in the paper (compute time scales roughly linearly with dataset size).

Because fitting is stochastic, results differ slightly across random seeds. Fit several models (the paper used ~20) and rank them with the "expected marginal likelihood" score described in the paper to select — or build a consensus from — the best-fitting run, rather than trusting a single fit.

For downstream analysis, the package's built-in analysis pipeline covers syllable transition graphs, grid movies of each syllable, and group comparisons (for example a Kruskal-Wallis test for syllables that differ significantly in frequency between conditions) — see the "analysis" section of the docs linked above.
tutorial_output: Per-frame syllable labels (the discrete behavioral state active at each timepoint, typically ~25-50 distinct syllables for a standard open-field session), a denoised/inferred pose trajectory that's robust to keypoint jitter and brief occlusions, and model diagnostics (the fitted transition matrix and per-syllable duration distribution) — each syllable corresponds to a recognizable, sub-second-to-second movement motif such as a rear, turn, or grooming bout.

sample_data.text: The paper benchmarks against the public CalMS21 mouse social-behavior dataset (keypoints plus human-annotated social behaviors: mounting, investigation, attack).

title: Foundation model of neural activity predicts response to new stimulus types
authors: Wang E.Y., Fahey P.G., Ding Z., Papadopoulos S., Ponder K., Weis M.A., et al., Sinz F.H., Tolias A.S.
summary: A deep neural network "foundation model" trained on responses from around 135,000 mouse visual-cortex neurons across 8 mice, whose frozen shared "core" lets new mice be fitted with minimal data and generalizes to out-of-distribution stimuli (Gabor filters, flashing dots, random-dot kinematograms) — and whose per-neuron "functional barcodes" predict anatomical cell type, dendritic morphology, and synaptic connectivity in the MICrONS connectomics dataset.
abstract_long: The model is an ANN with four modules: a perspective module that uses ray tracing plus eye-tracking to infer what the mouse's retina actually sees from the raw stimulus and pupil position; a modulation module (a small LSTM) that turns locomotion and pupil-size signals into a dynamic behavioral-state representation; a core module (feedforward 3D-convolutional layers plus recurrent Conv-LSTM or CvT-LSTM cells) that produces the bulk of the model's nonlinear visual representation; and a readout module that linearly maps the core's output, at each neuron's own learned spatial position, onto that neuron's predicted response. Trained end-to-end on natural-video responses from a "foundation cohort" of 8 mice, the resulting shared core could be frozen and transferred to new mice, requiring far less new data (well under 30 minutes) than training a model from scratch to reach the same accuracy — and this advantage held not just for natural videos but for stimulus types never seen during training, including drifting Gabors, flashing Gaussian dots, directional pink noise, and random-dot kinematograms. Applied to the MICrONS dataset (which pairs functional recordings with nanometer-resolution electron microscopy across a 1 mm3 volume), each neuron's fitted readout — a spatial position plus a 512-dimensional "functional barcode" of feature weights — accurately predicted its visual area and, from a separate logistic-regression classifier, its morphologically defined excitatory cell type, substantially above chance and beyond what could be explained by imaging depth alone. The same functional barcodes were used in companion papers to predict synaptic connectivity and dendritic morphology from function alone.
data_acquisition: Two-photon calcium imaging (large field-of-view mesoscope) of roughly 135,000 excitatory neurons across mouse visual cortex, recorded during natural-video and parametric visual stimulation, paired with eye-tracking and treadmill locomotion data
animal: Mouse
tutorial_intro: The work is split across three repos mirroring the pipeline: cajal/pipeline (raw two-photon calcium imaging plus eye/behavior processing), cajal/foundation (model training and downstream analyses), and cajal/fnn (the released model architecture and pretrained foundation weights, linked as the main GitHub above). If you just want to use the pretrained foundation core to predict responses or run in silico experiments on new stimuli, cajal/fnn is the relevant starting point rather than reproducing data collection and training from scratch.
tutorial_steps: Start from cajal/fnn if you want to use the released pretrained foundation core; only clone cajal/pipeline and cajal/foundation as well if you need to reproduce calcium-imaging preprocessing or full model training from raw recordings.

Prepare your inputs in the format the architecture expects: synchronized stimulus video frames, eye position (for the perspective/ray-tracing module), and behavioral variables (treadmill locomotion speed, pupil diameter and its instantaneous derivative, for the modulation module) — the same four input streams described in the paper's architecture.

To fit a new mouse using transfer learning (the paper's "foundation model" approach, as opposed to training an "individual model" from scratch): freeze the pretrained shared core and fit only the perspective, modulation, and readout modules using a natural-video recording session from your own mouse — the paper found this reached high accuracy with well under 30 minutes of new data, versus over an hour for training all four modules end-to-end.

To run in silico experiments — for example, reproducing classical parametric-tuning measurements (orientation/direction selectivity, spatial receptive fields) without presenting those stimuli in vivo — pass synthetic stimuli (drifting Gabor filters, flashing Gaussian dots, directional pink noise, random-dot kinematograms) through your fitted model and read out the predicted per-neuron responses, then fit the same parametric tuning models described in the paper's Methods (a mixture of von Mises functions for orientation/direction, a 2D Gaussian for spatial receptive fields).

Extract each neuron's fitted readout — a 2D spatial position (its receptive-field center within the core's feature maps) and a 512-dimensional feature-weight vector, together forming a "functional barcode" — directly from a fitted model for downstream analyses, such as training your own classifier to relate function to anatomy.

To relate model outputs to anatomy or connectivity (as in the paper's MICrONS analysis), separately obtain the corresponding connectomics/morphology data (see the MICrONS data link above) and match neurons via their functional-to-structural coregistration IDs.
tutorial_output: Predicted per-neuron response time series for arbitrary visual stimuli, in-domain or out-of-domain; a per-neuron "functional barcode" (readout spatial position plus 512-dimensional feature-weight vector) usable to predict anatomical properties such as visual area, cell type, dendritic morphology, or synaptic connectivity; and, for parametric stimuli, fitted tuning parameters (orientation/direction selectivity indices and preferred angles, spatial selectivity index and preferred receptive-field location) directly comparable to in vivo measurements.

sample_data.text: The MICrONS functional and connectomics data used in the paper's structure-function analyses are publicly hosted, browsable via the MICrONS Explorer or accessible in bulk from BossDB.

extra_links.label: cajal/pipeline (experimental recording and calcium-imaging processing pipeline)

title: Projection-TAGs enable multiplex projection tracing and multi-modal profiling of projection neurons
authors: Yang L., Liu F., Hahm H., Okuda T., Li X., Zhang Y., Kalyanaraman V., Heitmeier M.R., Samineni V.K.
summary: Projection-TAGs is a retrograde AAV platform that tags projection neurons with unique RNA barcodes so that multiple projections can be traced simultaneously and profiled with commercial single-cell/spatial assays (snRNA-seq, snATAC-seq, multiplexed FISH), letting researchers build multi-modal maps of projection neuron transcriptomes, chromatin accessibility, and spatial organization without specialized sequencing instruments.
abstract_long: The authors engineered a set of retrograde AAV2-retro vectors, each expressing a unique 100-nt RNA barcode ("Projection-TAG") fused to Sun1-GFP, so that injecting a different barcoded virus into each of several downstream target regions retrogradely labels neurons in the source region according to which target(s) they project to — detectable via standard commercial assays (snRNA-seq, snATAC-seq, multiplexed FISH) rather than custom sequencing pipelines. Applied to seven projection targets of mouse motor and somatosensory cortex, Projection-TAGs revealed the spatial distribution of distinct projection populations, extensive axonal collaterals (30.6% of labeled neurons expressed more than one TAG), and — by integrating snRNA-seq with snATAC-seq — thousands of putative cell-type-specific and projection-specific enhancers and silencers. The authors also show Projection-TAGs can capture activity-dependent recruitment of specific projections (via Act-seq) following an acute visceral-pain stimulus.
data_acquisition: Retrograde AAV2-retro RNA-barcode labeling (custom "Projection-TAG" plasmids) combined with single-nucleus RNA-seq, single-nucleus ATAC-seq, and multiplexed FISH
language: R (regulatory-element analysis); command-line tools (cellranger-based read mapping)
animal: Mouse
tutorial_intro: This repo is analysis code for reproducing the paper's own bioinformatic pipeline (barcode read mapping and regulatory-element identification) rather than the wet-lab protocol itself — the actual "tool" is largely a set of AAV plasmids (available from Addgene) plus a detection workflow using standard commercial single-cell/spatial assays. Expect to design your own retrograde-tracing experiment (choosing target regions, TAGs, and downstream assay) and use this repo's scripts for the sequencing-analysis side.
tutorial_steps: For Projection-TAG read mapping: generate a custom cellranger reference genome that includes the Projection-TAG sequences as additional "genes," then map your snRNA-seq/snATAC-seq reads to this custom reference using cellranger as normal — this lets you read out each cell's Projection-TAG expression exactly like any other gene in your standard single-cell analysis pipeline.

Determine which cells are positive for each projection by thresholding Projection-TAG UMI counts per nucleus (the paper used an FDR cutoff of 0.34%, estimated from the false-detection rate observed in empty droplets and non-neuronal cells in their own data — recompute this threshold for your own dataset rather than assuming it transfers directly).

For identifying putative genomic regulatory elements (GREs): using paired snRNA-seq (gene expression) and snATAC-seq (chromatin accessibility) data from the same cell populations, follow the repo's R scripts to (1) get expression/accessibility values for differentially expressed genes and differentially accessible peaks per cell type or projection, (2) calculate the Pearson correlation between every gene-peak pair within a 5 Mbp window on the same chromosome, and (3) classify strongly positively correlated pairs (r > 0.75) as putative enhancer-gene pairs and strongly negatively correlated pairs (r < -0.75) as putative silencer-gene pairs.

If you're designing your own multiplex tracing experiment rather than reanalyzing this paper's data, note the practical considerations the authors report: Projection-TAG detection is efficient but not exhaustive in snRNA-seq (a substantial false-negative rate — a cell lacking TAG expression does not necessarily lack that projection), transduction efficiency isn't perfectly uniform across projection pathways, and multiplexed FISH gives higher per-cell detection sensitivity than sequencing at the cost of being far more labor-intensive to scale.
tutorial_output: Per-nucleus Projection-TAG expression calls (which of your labeled projection targets, if any, that cell projects to) integrated into a standard snRNA-seq/snATAC-seq analysis, and — from the regulatory-element pipeline — tables of putative cell-type-specific and projection-specific enhancer-gene and silencer-gene pairs with their supporting correlation statistics.

title: Inter-brain neural dynamics in biological and artificial intelligence systems
authors: Zhang X., Phi N., Li Q., Gorzek R., Zwingenberger N., Huang S., Zhou J.L., Kingsbury L., Raam T., Wu Y.E., Wei D., Kao J.C., Hong W.
summary: Using dual-mouse microendoscopic calcium imaging in the dmPFC plus multi-agent reinforcement learning, the authors show GABAergic neurons carry a much larger "shared neural subspace" across interacting individuals than glutamatergic neurons, and that disrupting the analogous shared dimensions in AI agents impairs their social behavior.
abstract_long: The authors recorded calcium activity simultaneously from molecularly defined glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons in the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC) of pairs of freely interacting mice. Using partial least squares correlation (PLSC), they partitioned each mouse's neural activity into a "shared neural subspace" (dynamics correlated across the two brains) and a "unique neural subspace" (activity specific to one animal). GABAergic neurons — despite being a minority cell type — contained a substantially larger shared subspace than glutamatergic neurons, driven by both self- and partner-behavior representations, especially during mutual aggressive interactions. The authors then trained multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) agents in a simple chaser-explorer environment and found that shared neural dynamics analogous to those in mice emerged between interacting agents as social behavior developed; computationally removing the shared dimensions from an agent's recurrent network substantially reduced its social actions (collisions, keeping the partner in view), establishing a causal role for shared neural dynamics in driving social interaction.
data_acquisition: In vivo microendoscopic calcium imaging (Miniscope V4, GRIN lens) — cell-type-specific GCaMP6f (CaMKII-GCaMP6f for glutamatergic, mDlx-GCaMP6f for GABAergic neurons) recorded simultaneously in two freely interacting mice in the dmPFC
animal: Mouse
tutorial_intro: Like other multi-modal systems neuroscience papers, this isn't one installable tool but a set of separate repos, most under the hongw-lab GitHub account, each handling one stage of the pipeline (behavior annotation, pose tracking, calcium imaging preprocessing, ensemble detection, or the MARL environment). The repo linked above as the main one is specifically the analysis code for reproducing this paper's own figures (PLSC, shared/unique subspace analyses); the others are more general-purpose supporting tools.
tutorial_steps: Raw calcium videos from paired Miniscopes are first motion-corrected with NoRMCorre, then run through CNMF-E (constrained non-negative matrix factorization tuned for the large, non-uniform background typical of endoscopic 1-photon imaging) to extract per-cell fluorescence traces — both are standalone MATLAB tools usable on any similar dataset, not specific to this paper.

Animal behavior was annotated two ways: manually, using the lab's own behavior_annotator tool (built on Piotr Dollar's MATLAB toolbox) for frame-by-frame labeling of a fixed behavior vocabulary (attack, sniff, approach, etc.), and automatically via posture tracking with SLEAP, a general-purpose multi-animal pose-tracking package — useful on its own if you just need tracking, independent of the manual annotation step.

Once you have per-cell calcium traces and behavior annotations for two simultaneously recorded animals, the paper-specific repo (linked above) implements the core PLSC (partial least squares correlation) analysis that partitions each animal's neural activity into shared and unique subspaces — this is the part you'd actually want to adapt if you're trying to reproduce or extend the paper's specific inter-brain analysis on your own two-animal calcium imaging dataset.

For identifying intra-brain neural ensembles (correlated groups of neurons within one animal), the repo uses a separate PCA-ICA-based cell assembly detection tool, linked above, which is also usable independently for single-brain ensemble analysis.

The multi-agent reinforcement learning side is a separate, self-contained pipeline: a chaser-explorer environment built on Ray/RLlib (linked above), trained with PPO. If you want to test whether "shared neural dynamics" emerge in your own multi-agent RL setup, you'd apply the same PLSC analysis (from the main repo) to the agents' RNN hidden-unit activations instead of calcium traces — the underlying math is identical, only the source of "neural" activity changes.
tutorial_output: Depends on the stage: the imaging pipeline (NoRMCorre + CNMF-E) outputs per-cell calcium fluorescence traces per animal; the PLSC analysis outputs a set of "shared neural dimensions" (with per-dimension correlation/covariance across the two animals) and a complementary "unique neural subspace" per animal, plus the fraction of neural variance each accounts for; the MARL pipeline outputs trained agent policies and, when combined with the same PLSC analysis applied to RNN activations, the equivalent shared/unique dimension breakdown for artificial agents. The paper's own source data (underlying all figures) is provided as supplementary files alongside the publication rather than a separate code repository.

extra_links.label: Piotr Dollar's MATLAB toolbox (used for behavior annotation)
CNMF-E (constrained NMF for endoscopic data extraction)

title: JAX Animal Behavior System (JABS), a genetics-informed, end-to-end advanced behavioral phenotyping platform for the laboratory mouse
authors: Choudhary A., Geuther B.Q., Sproule T.J., Beane G., Kohar V., Trapszo J., Kumar V.
summary: End-to-end platform for mouse behavior phenotyping: standardized video hardware, an active-learning GUI for training pose-based behavior classifiers, and a web app for classifier sharing plus heritability/genetic-correlation analysis across 168 strains.
abstract_long: JABS integrates three components into a single open-source ecosystem for behavioral neurogenetics. JABS-DA provides standardized 3D-printable hardware and software for uniform day/night video collection. JABS-AL is a Python GUI for annotating behaviors and training pose-based classifiers (Random Forest / XGBoost), including a new graph-based method ("ethograph") for comparing classifiers bout-by-bout instead of frame-by-frame, which better captures inter-annotator agreement. JABS-AI is a web application where users upload trained classifiers, run them against three public strain-survey datasets (JABS600, JABS1200, JABS-BxD; 168 strains total), and receive heritability and genetic-correlation results automatically. The authors benchmark JABS-AL against a prior 3D-CNN grooming classifier, reaching comparable accuracy (0.936 vs 0.937) with roughly 10x less labeled data, and demonstrate the ethograph approach on left/right-turn classifiers built by two different annotators.
data_acquisition: Top-down IR video, custom open-field arena (Basler acA1300-75gm camera, 800x800px/30fps)
animal: Mouse

subjects.notes: Only single-animal tracking is released; GitHub repo states the multi-mouse pose model is not out yet, so it's unclear if a future multi-animal mode will need distinct strains for identity.

tutorial_intro: Input data: a project folder of videos with matching pose files (HDF5, v2-v4) produced by the companion mouse-tracking-runtime pipeline. JABS itself doesn't run pose estimation — it assumes keypoints already exist for every video in the project, one pose file per video, following the naming convention the tracking pipeline outputs. Raw video is only needed for the manual labeling step, since features for classification are computed from the pose data, not pixels.
tutorial_steps: Install the classifier package: pipx install jabs-behavior-classifier (or uv tool install jabs-behavior-classifier if you prefer uv's tool manager). Both install JABS as an isolated CLI/GUI application rather than into your active Python environment, which avoids dependency conflicts with other pose/behavior tools you might have installed.

Point JABS at your project folder, which should contain your videos alongside their matching pose HDF5 files. Before labeling anything, it's worth pre-computing features for the whole project in parallel: jabs-init project_dir -p 8 (the -p flag sets how many videos to process concurrently). This computes the same per-frame feature set the classifier will train on — distances, angles, and kinematic descriptors derived from the keypoints — up front, which is considerably faster than letting the GUI compute them lazily the first time you hit Train.

Open the project in the JABS GUI and define a new behavior (give it a name — this becomes the label for the classifier you're about to train). Label bouts by scrubbing through a video with the arrow keys and marking frames with three keys: z for "behavior is occurring," c for "behavior is not occurring," and x to clear a mislabeled frame. JABS uses an active-learning loop, so you don't need to exhaustively label an entire video — the GUI will suggest which additional frames would be most informative to label next as your classifier improves.

Once you've reached the minimum labeling threshold (100 labeled frames spread across at least 2 different videos), the Train button becomes available. Choose a classifier type — Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, or XGBoost — and use the built-in cross-validation slider to check how well the classifier generalizes to held-out labeled frames before trusting it on new data. If accuracy looks poor, the usual fix is adding more labels, particularly for behavior variants or camera angles that were underrepresented in your initial labeling pass.

Once you're satisfied with classifier performance, export the behavior definition for safekeeping or sharing via File → Export Training Data, which writes a <behavior>_training_<timestamp>.h5 file containing the trained model plus the labels used to build it. To apply the trained classifier to new, unlabeled videos in bulk rather than one at a time in the GUI, use the command-line interface: jabs-classify classify --training TRAINING.h5 --input-pose POSE.h5 --out-dir OUT_DIR, which is the more practical route once you're scoring many videos.
tutorial_output: Two kinds of output: a portable *_training_<timestamp>.h5 file that fully defines your trained classifier (shareable with collaborators, or re-usable later without re-labeling), and per-video HDF5 inference files produced by jabs-classify containing, per frame, the predicted_class (behavior present/absent), a probabilities score reflecting classifier confidence, and identity_to_track mapping predictions back to a specific animal in multi-animal videos. These per-video files are what you'd feed into downstream ethogram analysis, or upload to the JABS-AI web app if you want automatic heritability and genetic-correlation results against the public strain-survey datasets.

sample_data.text: Public strain-survey datasets (JABS600, JABS1200, JABS-BxD) with matching keypoint files, hosted on Harvard Dataverse.

title: Neural basis of compositional control
authors: Chericoni A., Fine J.M., Ismail T.S., Delgado Salazar G., Franch M.C., et al.
summary: Human intracranial recordings during a continuous prey-pursuit task, decomposed via a novel control-theoretic model into blended goal-specific policies, show ACC predicting policy-blend switches, hippocampus encoding and updating the latent policy state, and OFC signaling task value rather than driving the switching itself.
abstract_long: The authors recorded single neurons from anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), hippocampus (HPC) and orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) via stereotactic EEG in 19 epilepsy patients performing a continuous, joystick-controlled prey-pursuit task, plus behavioral-only data from 50 healthy participants. They developed a control-theoretic decomposition that models pursuit behavior as a meta-controller dynamically blending several lower-level, goal-specific control policies (a continuous analogue of discrete choice). Fitting this model to behavior, they found ACC neurons predict upcoming major changes in the policy blend (akin to a "change of mind"), hippocampal neurons encode and update the latent policy-blend state supporting early planning, and OFC activity tracks the task's current value structure rather than the switching process itself — supporting a tripartite division of labor: hippocampus as state estimator, ACC as meta-controller, OFC as value-context signal.
data_acquisition: Human single-neuron intracranial recordings — stereotactic EEG (sEEG) via AdTech Behnke-Fried microwire probes (~4 probes/patient, 8 microwires each), Blackrock Neuroport 512-channel system at 30 kHz, spike-sorted with WaveClus
animal: Not applicable (human intracranial recordings in epilepsy patients)
tutorial_intro: Input data: for the behavioral controller-modeling step, per-trial joystick trajectories and prey positions; for the neural analyses (GAM tuning, dPCA, clustering), spike-sorted single-unit firing rates aligned to those same trials, organized per participant. The repo includes real example data for one participant plus synthetic data for the population-level demos, so you can run every step below without your own dataset first.
tutorial_steps: Set up the environment: conda env create -f environment.yml, then conda activate pac_control_env, then pip install --no-build-isolation "ssm @ git+https://github.com/lindermanlab/ssm" (the ssm package needs to be installed separately via pip). On Windows you'll also need Visual Studio C++ Build Tools v14.0.0 or newer.

Run the behavioral controller-modeling pipeline: python -m scripts.run_controller_modeling -c pv, where -c selects a controller class (options: p, pv, pf, pvi, pif, pvf — pv was the best-fitting class in the paper). This fits the control-theoretic decomposition to a participant's trial-by-trial behavior and takes about 15 minutes to run.

For model recovery (checking whether the fitting procedure correctly recovers known ground-truth controller parameters from simulated data), see demo/simulation_demo.ipynb — full recovery runs are slow, so example results and MATLAB plotting scripts for this step are pre-computed under plotting/simulation.

For detecting behavioral "changes of mind" (major switches in the policy blend) from the fitted wt trajectories, use the functions in ChangeOfMind/functions/processing.py, demonstrated in demo/plot_switch_detection.ipynb — this runs directly on the output of the controller-modeling step above.

For relating neural firing to the fitted policy-blend variable (wt) via generalized additive models: python -m scripts.run_glm_modeling -p YFD (participant ID; optionally add -m <controller_class> to specify which fitted wt to use). Plot the proportion of tuned neurons, NNMF results, and Fisher information with plotting/plot_nmf_fi.ipynb.

For the demixed PCA (dPCA) population analysis (condition-based and wt-binned), the pipeline lives in src/dPCA via the DPCAPipeline class, demonstrated with synthetic data in demo/dPCA_demo_Final.ipynb; plotting scripts are in plotting/MAIN_plot_dPCA_results.m (MATLAB).

For clustering neurons by their ramping/dynamical behavior around switches, the LDS (linear dynamical system) + k-means pipeline is in scripts/lds_cluster_pipeline.py, demonstrated on single-subject data in demo/run_lds_cluster_pipeline_demo.ipynb — the full pipeline is designed to run on pseudopopulations pooled across subjects.
tutorial_output: The controller-modeling step writes model_fit_results.csv (fitted controller weights and the model's evidence lower bound, ELBO) and model_matrices.mat (the trial-wise wt — policy-blend — time series) into example_data/<participant>/<controller>/. Downstream steps consume these: the switch-detection step outputs detected change-of-mind events per trial; the GAM modeling step outputs per-neuron tuning statistics to wt; the dPCA step outputs low-dimensional population components capturing how neural activity varies with time and policy-blend state; and the LDS+k-means step outputs cluster assignments describing distinct classes of single-neuron ramping dynamics around switches.

sample_data.text: The repo ships with real example behavioral + neural data from one participant, plus synthetic pseudopopulation datasets, so the full pipeline can be run end to end without needing your own recordings first.

title: CellExplorer: A framework for visualizing and characterizing single neurons
authors: Petersen P.C., Siegle J.H., Steinmetz N.A., Mahallati S., Buzsáki G.
summary: Turns spike-sorted extracellular recordings into standardized physiological metrics and helps classify units into cell types (e.g. pyramidal cells, interneurons) via a MATLAB GUI.
data_acquisition: Extracellular electrophysiology — silicon probes / Neuropixels (IMEC)
animal: Mouse, rat
tutorial_intro: CellExplorer expects data you've already spike-sorted with a tool like KiloSort followed by manual curation in Phy. Organize each recording session in its own folder named after the session ("basepath"), containing the raw .dat file, the spike times/cluster ID outputs from your sorter, and the probe/channel-map metadata for that session. If you're working with several sessions from the same animal, keep each in its own basepath folder rather than combining them.
tutorial_steps: Add CellExplorer to your MATLAB path (clone or download the repo, then addpath(genpath('CellExplorer'))). CellExplorer builds on functions from Buzcode/Neurosuite-style pipelines, so make sure your sorted data follows that basic session structure before continuing.

Generate the session metadata file: session = sessionTemplate(basepath, 'showGUI', true). This opens a small GUI where you confirm details CellExplorer needs to interpret your recording correctly — probe geometry/channel map, sampling rate, and basic experiment metadata (animal, date, epochs if the session has multiple behavioral epochs). Getting this step right matters: an incorrect channel map will make waveform-based metrics meaningless downstream.

Run the main processing pipeline: cell_metrics = ProcessCellMetrics('session', session). This is the computational core of the tool — for every sorted unit it computes the mean waveform and derived shape metrics (trough-to-peak time, waveform asymmetry), firing-rate statistics (mean rate, burstiness, ISI distribution), the autocorrelogram, and putative monosynaptic connections to other units in the same session based on cross-correlogram features. Processing time scales with the number of units and session length — expect anywhere from a couple of minutes for a small session to tens of minutes for large multi-shank recordings.

Launch the interactive GUI to inspect and curate the results: cell_metrics = CellExplorer('metrics', cell_metrics). The GUI shows, per unit, the waveform, autocorrelogram, firing-rate stability over the session, and its position in a low-dimensional feature space alongside other units. CellExplorer proposes an initial cell-type label (for example, Pyramidal Cell, Narrow Interneuron, Wide Interneuron) based on waveform and firing statistics, which you can accept or manually override — useful when you have independent evidence (for example, optogenetic tagging) that overrides the automatic call.

If you're working across multiple sessions from the same study, load them together for batch curation instead of one at a time: cell_metrics = loadCellMetricsBatch('basepaths', {basepath1, basepath2, ...}). This lets you browse and classify units from all sessions in a single GUI session and keeps your classification criteria consistent across the dataset.

Optionally, compare your units against CellExplorer's shared reference database of previously characterized neurons from other labs — useful as a sanity check on whether your waveform/firing metrics fall within expected ranges for a given cell type, and for benchmarking an unusual-looking unit against known examples.
tutorial_output: The main output is a cell_metrics.mat file (or one per session, plus a combined batch object) containing, per unit: waveform shape features, firing-rate and ISI statistics, autocorrelogram-derived features, putative monosynaptic connection partners, and a final cell-type label (pyramidal cell, narrow interneuron, or wide interneuron, refined into further subtypes in later CellExplorer versions) that you confirmed or edited in the GUI. The GUI also lets you export publication-ready waveform, ACG, and connectivity figures directly, and you can save your manual classification decisions back into the cell_metrics structure so they persist for downstream analysis scripts.

title: Imaging cellular activity across all organs reveals body-wide circuits
authors: Ruetten V.M.S., Zheng W., Siwanowicz I., Mensh B.D., Eddison M., et al.
summary: WHOLISTIC is a whole-body live-imaging platform recording second-timescale calcium activity across nearly every cell type in a transparent vertebrate, paired with a registration/segmentation/clustering computational pipeline and whole-body expansion microscopy for anatomical follow-up.
abstract_long: The authors built a pancellular calcium-imaging platform (WHOLISTIC) combining a transgenic zebrafish line expressing GCaMP7f in essentially all cells, high-speed volumetric spinning-disk confocal microscopy, and a computational pipeline that corrects for the large, non-rigid tissue motion caused by muscle contractions before segmenting and clustering cells into "functional tissue ensembles." Applying this across the body revealed previously unknown biology at multiple scales: chondrocyte responses to cold, meningeal responses to ketamine, rhythmic traveling calcium waves along the kidney nephron, an independent "cervical epaxial" muscle group, motor-quiescence-linked ultraslow oscillations traced to a previously uncharacterized population of long-projecting ependymal cells, and — combining WHOLISTIC with optogenetics — a causal brainstem-to-gut circuit that redirects blood flow away from the viscera during hypoxia. A new whole-body expansion microscopy protocol (WB-ExM) was developed alongside WHOLISTIC to validate cell identities and resolve fine anatomy that live imaging alone couldn't.
data_acquisition: Volumetric fluorescence imaging — dual-color spinning-disk confocal microscopy (pancellular GCaMP7f/jRGECO1b calcium indicators plus an anatomical reference channel), ~0.3 Hz volumetric rate
animal: Zebrafish (larval), Danionella cerebrum (adult)
tutorial_intro: This is a suite of separate, focused tools rather than one installable package — each repo under the vruetten GitHub account handles one stage of the WHOLISTIC pipeline and is released with its own versioned Zenodo archive. Expect to read each repo's own README for exact usage, since a general-purpose whole-body imaging pipeline hasn't been formally published in one interface yet.
tutorial_steps: Start with wholistic_registration if your problem is non-rigid motion correction in volumetric fluorescence data — it corrects for tissue displacement caused by muscle contraction using patch-wise iterative optical flow with a multi-resolution image pyramid, and is designed to be GPU-parallelizable. It expects a "template" reference channel (something relatively stable, like an anatomical marker) alongside your signal channel of interest (for example, calcium), since the registration is computed on the stable channel and then applied to align the dynamic one.

Once your data is registered, cell-level signals are extracted with voluseg, a volumetric segmentation pipeline based on constrained non-negative matrix factorization — it takes registered volumetric time-series data and outputs per-cell fluorescence traces, tuned conservatively in this paper to over-segment rather than risk merging distinct cells.

To go from cellular calcium traces to interpretable "functional tissue ensembles," the paper uses coherence-based spectral clustering rather than plain correlation — grouping cells with temporally structured, possibly phase-lagged activity (like traveling waves) that correlation-based methods would miss. This part of the analysis isn't broken out as a standalone package in the code availability statement, so expect to implement the coherence-clustering step yourself following the Methods section if you want to reproduce it exactly.

If your goal is validating cell identities or resolving fine anatomical structures underlying a functional signal (as the ependymal-cell finding in this paper required), the whole-body expansion microscopy protocol and its PhotoMap tool are the relevant pieces — PhotoMap quantifies the physical deformation field introduced by the tissue-expansion process itself, using a photobleached reference grid, so you can assess whether expansion was uniform before trusting downstream measurements.

For a purely anatomical starting point (for example, if you want a labeled 3D reference to register your own zebrafish data against, independent of building it yourself), the wholebodymodel repo provides the 3D geometric model of the young zebrafish body built from this paper's WB-ExM data.
tutorial_output: Output depends on which stage you use: wholistic_registration outputs a motion-corrected version of your volumetric time-series data plus the estimated per-frame displacement field; voluseg outputs per-cell fluorescence time series (and their spatial footprints) extracted from registered data; and PhotoMap outputs a quantified 3D deformation field describing how much and how uniformly a sample expanded, useful as a quality-control step before trusting expansion-microscopy-based measurements. Note: a specific raw-imaging-data repository wasn't identified in this indexing pass beyond the code releases above — check the paper's own Data Availability statement if you need the underlying imaging datasets rather than just the analysis code.

extra_links.label: Whole-body 3D geometric model from WB-ExM data

title: Topographic structure and function of locus coeruleus noradrenaline neurons
authors: Su Z., Kosillo P., Jung K., Chen S., Summers M.T., et al.
summary: Multi-modal Allen Institute study linking locus coeruleus noradrenaline neuron morphology, gene expression, and electrophysiological activity along a dorsal-ventral topography, with dorsal cortex-projecting neurons encoding choice switches and reward-prediction errors during a reinforcement-learning task.
abstract_long: Using whole-brain light-sheet imaging, the authors reconstructed complete axonal morphologies of individual locus coeruleus noradrenaline (LC-NE) neurons and found that projections are extensive but largely confined to specific brain regions, correlating with the dorsal-ventral position of the cell body. Single-nucleus RNA-seq showed gene expression is smoothly graded along the same axis. During a dynamic reward-learning task, electrophysiological recordings (with optogenetic tagging) showed that dorsal LC-NE neurons projecting to isocortex were preferentially active when mice switched choices and encoded reward-prediction-error signals, while ventral neurons showed higher background activity when mice ignored reward-predictive cues — linking anatomical, molecular, and functional topography in a major neuromodulatory system.
data_acquisition: Multi-modal — whole-brain light-sheet imaging (ExA-SPIM) for single-neuron reconstruction, electrophysiology (Neuropixels probes/tetrodes) with optogenetic tagging, snRNA-seq, MAPseq/BARseq projection mapping, fiber photometry
animal: Mouse
tutorial_intro: This project spans several modalities (whole-brain anatomy, electrophysiology, transcriptomics, projection mapping, behavior), so the code is deliberately split across the main repo (linked above) plus a few supporting infrastructure repos rather than one single pipeline you install and run end-to-end. The CodeOcean capsule collection (linked as the website above) has containerized, reproducible versions of the analyses if you want to rerun a specific figure without setting up each modality's environment yourself from scratch.
tutorial_steps: Start from the CodeOcean capsule collection (linked above) if your goal is to reproduce a specific figure without installing dependencies — each capsule bundles the code, environment, and (where feasible) the data for one part of the analysis, so you can launch it and inspect the outputs without local setup.

For the main repo, clone AllenNeuralDynamics/locus_coeruleus_norepinephrine_neurons and check its own README for the specific analysis scripts, since the repo is organized by modality (anatomy/morphology, electrophysiology, and behavior each have their own subdirectories with separate environments).

If your interest is specifically in projection mapping via barcoded RNA sequencing (MAPseq/BARseq), that step is handled by a standalone tool rather than the main repo: ZadorLaboratory/mapseq-processing takes the raw paired-end FASTQ output from a MAPseq/BARseq run and produces barcode-to-brain-region projection matrices — useful independently of this specific paper if you're running your own barcoded projection-mapping experiment.

If you're after the whole-brain light-sheet image registration and stitching pipeline used for the single-neuron reconstructions, that's AllenNeuralDynamics/aind-smartspim-pipeline — it handles registering ExA-SPIM whole-brain volumes to the Allen Common Coordinate Framework (CCFv3), which is the anatomical reference space all the projection and soma-location results in this paper are expressed in.

For the reinforcement-learning models fit to mouse choice behavior during the dynamic-foraging task (the source of the reward-prediction-error estimates correlated with LC-NE activity), see AllenNeuralDynamics/aind-dynamic-foraging-models — it implements several RL agent classes (Q-learning, loss-counting, win-stay-lose-switch variants) that can be fit to any dataset following the same trial-structure convention, not just this paper's sessions.

Electrophysiology and fiber photometry data underlying the reward-related findings are on DANDI (linked under Sample data) in NWB format, which is a reasonable starting point if you want to explore the raw recordings without regenerating them yourself.
tutorial_output: Output format varies substantially by module, reflecting the different modalities: the anatomical pipeline outputs registered whole-brain image volumes and individual neuron reconstructions in SWC format (a standard neuron-morphology file format compatible with most morphology analysis tools); the MAPseq/BARseq pipeline outputs barcode-by-brain-region count matrices representing each labeled neuron's projection pattern; and the behavioral models output fitted reinforcement-learning parameters (learning rates, choice-kernel weights) plus trial-by-trial reward-prediction-error estimates that can be correlated against neural recordings, as done in the paper's main electrophysiology analysis.

sample_data.text: Electrophysiology and fiber photometry data from the dynamic foraging task, deposited on DANDI (Dandiset 001950).

extra_links.label: Dynamic foraging behavioral models (RL agents used for choice/RPE analysis)

title: Reciprocal connections dynamically build consensus between neocortical areas
authors: Javadzadeh M., Schimel M., Hofer S.B., Ahmadian Y., Hennequin G.
summary: Using iLQR-VAE — a control-based variational method that jointly infers latent circuit dynamics and unobserved trial-by-trial external inputs — the authors fit biologically constrained excitation-inhibition circuit models to simultaneous V1-LM recordings and optogenetic perturbations, finding that reciprocal long-range excitatory connections between the two areas create an approximate line attractor that dynamically builds consensus between them about both the presence and identity of a visual stimulus.
abstract_long: The authors built latent circuit models of joint V1-LM dynamics constrained to reflect known cortical circuit organization: separate excitatory/inhibitory subpopulations within each area (Dale's law), with only excitatory units projecting across areas, and neurons assigned a definite E or I identity via a structured sparsity penalty. Trial-by-trial external inputs (visual stimulus and optogenetic perturbation) were inferred per trial using iLQR-VAE, a control-based sequential variational autoencoder that uses the iterative linear-quadratic-regulator algorithm as its recognition model. Fitted models generalized across animals, correctly labeled directly photo-stimulated PV+ interneurons as inhibitory in most fits, and predicted the effect of held-out optogenetic perturbations on unperturbed neurons — validation that the constrained circuit structure reflects real biology rather than an arbitrary parameterization. The fitted dynamics revealed that sustained visual responses depend on long-range (not local) recurrent connections, and that these reciprocal excitatory connections between V1 and LM create an approximate "line attractor": activity patterns where the two areas agree decay slowly, while patterns where they disagree decay quickly. A minimal, hand-derived E-I circuit model reproduced this mechanism analytically and showed it extends naturally to stimulus-identity consensus (not just stimulus-presence consensus) when connections carry feature-specific structure. Predictions of the model — that "agreeing" activity patterns should have longer autocorrelation timescales than "disagreeing" ones, and that silencing one area should speed up fluctuations in the other — were confirmed directly in the neural data, independent of the fitted model itself.
data_acquisition: Simultaneous multi-channel electrophysiological recordings from V1 and higher-order area LM in head-fixed mice performing a visual go/no-go task, with brief optogenetic silencing (PV+ interneuron activation) of one area on a subset of trials
animal: Mouse
tutorial_intro: iLQR-VAE is a general-purpose method for learning input-driven latent dynamics from neural population recordings — this paper's specific circuit constraints (E-I structure, area partitioning, cross-area excitation-only connections) are a particular application of it, implemented on top of the base iLQR-VAE package rather than shipped as a separate turnkey tool.
tutorial_steps: Install iLQR-VAE from the linked repository (a JAX-based Python package) and review the base method's own examples before adapting it to a multi-area or circuit-constrained setting like this paper's.

Prepare your data as binned spike counts (this paper used 5 ms bins) per neuron per trial, along with any known trial-structured external events you want the model to condition on (for example, stimulus onset/offset times, or optogenetic perturbation windows) — these inform the time-varying prior variance placed on each input channel, per equation (6) of the paper, rather than being fed to the model as hard-coded inputs.

Define your latent circuit's structure: the paper partitions latent units into areas and, within each area, into excitatory/inhibitory subpopulations, constraining the recurrent weight matrix so only excitatory units project across areas (their equation 10) — adapt this block structure to whatever circuit hypothesis you want to test, or omit it entirely for an unconstrained baseline model to check whether your constraints hurt model fit.

If you want neurons to be assigned an unambiguous cell-type identity (as this paper does for excitatory vs. inhibitory), add a structured sparsity penalty on the readout matrix (their equation 12) that discourages a neuron from loading onto both an excitatory and inhibitory latent subpopulation simultaneously.

Fit the model by maximizing the evidence lower bound (ELBO) via iLQR-VAE's control-based recognition model, which solves for the most likely trial-specific input trajectory using the iterative LQR algorithm rather than a separate encoder network.

Select hyperparameters (number of latent units, number of input channels) via cross-validation on held-out trials, and validate the fitted model with domain-specific checks where available — this paper used the known identity of directly photo-stimulated PV+ interneurons and the model's ability to predict held-out optogenetic perturbation effects as two such checks; reject or refit models that fail these checks.

To probe the resulting circuit's dynamics (for example, testing for a line attractor or characterizing relaxation timescales), linearize the fitted nonlinear dynamics around a period of interest and examine the eigenvalues/eigenvectors of the resulting linear system, or systematically down-scale specific connectivity blocks (for example, long-range vs. local) and measure the resulting change in the network's response.
tutorial_output: A fitted latent circuit model per animal, with inferred trial-specific external input trajectories, a decoded excitatory/inhibitory identity per recorded neuron, and — from downstream analysis of the fitted dynamics — relaxation time constants, eigenmode decompositions, and predicted responses to novel (including held-out or simulated) perturbations, usable to test specific circuit-mechanistic hypotheses about how the recorded areas interact.

title: Massively parallel assessment of gene regulatory activity at human cortical-structure-associated variants
authors: Matoba N., McAfee J.C., Krupa O., Beltran A.A., Bell J.L., Le B.D., Valone J.M., Min H., Crawford G.E., Raab J.R., Won H., Stein J.L.
summary: A massively parallel reporter assay (MPRA) testing the regulatory activity of over 9,000 human cortical-structure-associated genetic variants in neural progenitor cells, identifying hundreds of "expression-modulating variants" (emVars) — many driven by Alu-element-derived Pol III promoter elements and sensitive to Wnt-pathway stimulation — with the barcode-mapping and CUT&RUN analysis code released alongside it.
abstract_long: The authors designed an MPRA testing four sets of 150-bp DNA elements in primary human neural progenitor cells (phNPCs): positive-control promoters, caQTL-overlapping elements, elements centered on 9,092 variants from 198 ENIGMA GWAS loci associated with human cortical surface area or thickness, and scrambled negative controls. Regulatory activity (transcription rate relative to negative controls) and allelic effects (differences between the two alleles of a variant) were quantified via barcoded RNA/DNA sequencing, at baseline and after Wnt-pathway stimulation with CHIR99021. They found that 76% of tested loci contained at least one element with detectable regulatory activity, and more than half of regulatory variants showed significant allelic effects (emVars). Regulatory activity was strongly driven by Alu retrotransposons — specifically their left-arm RNA polymerase III promoter elements (A and B boxes) — with younger, less-diverged Alu elements showing higher activity, and CUT&RUN confirmed endogenous TFIIIC binding at these same elements in phNPCs. Disrupted transcription-factor motifs (notably RARA, RARG, ZNF135, and NR2F1) correlated with the strength of allelic effects, and the regional expression pattern of these TFs during prenatal cortical development helped explain why individual variants affect specific cortical regions rather than the whole cortex. A subset of variants showed Wnt-stimulation-dependent regulatory activity, and CRISPR interference at one such condition-dependent element (near FOXO3) experimentally confirmed its effect on endogenous gene expression.
data_acquisition: Massively parallel reporter assay (barcoded RNA/DNA sequencing) plus CUT&RUN chromatin profiling in primary human neural progenitor cells (phNPCs), at baseline and after Wnt-pathway (CHIR99021) stimulation
language: R (MPRAnalyze, mpra, limma, motifbreakR); Nextflow (CUT&RUN pipeline)
animal: Not applicable — human primary neural progenitor cells derived from fetal brain tissue
tutorial_intro: This isn't a general-purpose software package — it's the analysis code (barcode-to-variant mapping, and a separate CUT&RUN peak-calling pipeline) behind this specific MPRA screen. The core statistical analyses (regulatory activity, allelic effects) instead rely on established R/Bioconductor packages that you'd install directly rather than custom code from this paper.
tutorial_steps: If you're running your own MPRA experiment and need to map random barcodes to the variants/elements they tag, start from the linked thewonlab/schizophrenia-MPRA repo, which implements the barcode-mapping step described in the Methods (extracting 20-bp barcodes from paired-end sequencing reads and associating each with the oligo it was ligated to).

To quantify regulatory activity from your own RNA/DNA barcode counts, use the R/Bioconductor package MPRAnalyze — specifically its analyzeQuantification() function to estimate a transcription-rate parameter (α, adjusted for batch effects and library size) per element relative to your negative controls, as done in this paper.

To test for allelic effects (a difference in activity between two alleles of the same variant) or condition-dependent effects (activity differing between two experimental conditions), use the Bioconductor package mpra's mpralm() function followed by limma's topTable() — this paper's condition-dependent test additionally used a model with a genotype × condition interaction term.

To predict which transcription-factor binding motifs a variant disrupts, use the motifbreakR Bioconductor package against a JASPAR motif database (method = 'ic', threshold = 1e-4), filtering to motifs for TFs actually expressed in your cell type of interest; to scan more generally for motif matches within your reporter elements (not just at variant positions), use FIMO from the MEME Suite.

If you're processing your own CUT&RUN chromatin-profiling data, the raab-lab/cut-n-run Nextflow pipeline (linked above) implements this paper's alignment, quality-filtering, and peak-calling workflow, with deepTools (computeMatrix/plotHeatmap) for coverage visualization.

To annotate transposable elements (for example, Alu subfamilies) overlapping your reporter elements and estimate their relative evolutionary age, use the RepeatMasker annotation track from the UCSC Table Browser and stratify by the milliDiv divergence score, as done in this paper.
tutorial_output: Per-element regulatory activity scores (transcription rate relative to negative controls) and allelic-effect statistics (log-fold-change and FDR per variant) from the MPRA; predicted disrupted transcription-factor motifs per variant; and, from CUT&RUN, called peaks and coverage tracks for your transcription factor of interest — the building blocks this paper used to nominate causal variants, their target genes, and the transcription factors mediating their effects on cortical structure.
