title: Single-cell atlas of transcriptomic vulnerability across brain disorders
authors: Lee D., Koutrouli M., Masse N.Y., Hoffman G.E., Kinrot S., et al.
summary: A population-scale single-nucleus RNA-seq atlas of 1,494 human DLPFC donors spanning eight neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disorders, with code for cell-type composition, differential expression (dreamlet), and disease-trajectory analyses.
abstract_long: The authors generated a single-nucleus transcriptomic atlas of the human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex from 1,494 donors (over 6.3 million nuclei), covering neurotypical controls plus eight brain disorders: Alzheimer's disease, diffuse Lewy body disease, vascular dementia, Parkinson's disease, tauopathy, frontotemporal dementia, schizophrenia, and bipolar disorder. They quantify how much of the transcriptomic variation comes from cell type versus interindividual differences, identify gene expression signatures shared across disorders versus disease-specific ones, show that shared transcriptomic vulnerability tracks with genetic co-heritability between disorders, and model nonlinear gene-expression trajectories across Alzheimer's disease progression using neural networks trained on pathology and cognitive-decline measures.
data_acquisition: Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) — 10x Genomics Chromium, postmortem human DLPFC
animal: Not applicable (human postmortem tissue)

subjects.notes: Includes neurotypical controls and donors with Alzheimer's disease, diffuse Lewy body disease, vascular dementia, Parkinson's disease, tauopathy, frontotemporal dementia, schizophrenia, and bipolar disorder.

tutorial_intro: This repo is analysis code for reproducing the paper's own figures rather than a general-purpose tool you install and point at arbitrary data — it's organized into 9 numbered folders mirroring the paper's result sections in order, from raw metadata through to spatial validation. If your goal is to apply the paper's core statistical method to your own single-cell cohort rather than reproduce this specific paper, the reusable engine is the separate dreamlet R package (linked above), which is worth understanding on its own before diving into the paper-specific code.
tutorial_steps: Clone the repo. The 9 numbered folders correspond, in order, to: (1) metadata harmonization for the donor cohort, (2) preprocessing and hierarchical cellular taxonomy assignment from the raw snRNA-seq libraries, (3) partitioning transcriptomic variance into cell-type, donor, and technical sources, (4) compositional variation analysis across the eight disorders using the crumblr method, (5) differential gene expression across disorders using dreamlet's pseudobulk approach, (6) compositional and expression analysis specific to Alzheimer's disease pathology staging, (7) the neural-network-based disease trajectory modeling, (8) heritability analysis linking transcriptomic and genetic similarity between disorders, and (9) validation against spatial transcriptomics (MERFISH) data.

Set up your environment before running anything: R scripts require Bioconductor ≥3.17 with R ≥4.3.0, and Python scripts require Python ≥3.8. Each numbered folder has its own dependency list (typically at the top of the main script or in a folder-level README) — install per-folder rather than assuming one environment covers everything, since the R/Bioconductor and Python requirements differ meaningfully between the taxonomy/expression folders and the trajectory-modeling folder.

If you want to reuse the core differential-expression approach on your own pseudobulked single-cell dataset rather than reproducing this paper's specific disease comparisons, install dreamlet directly instead of going through this repo: devtools::install_github("DiseaseNeurogenomics/dreamlet"), then follow dreamlet's own documentation for fitting precision-weighted linear mixed models to your cohort. This is the more practical route if your actual goal is "run this kind of analysis on my data" rather than "reproduce this exact paper."

To reproduce a specific figure without starting from raw sequencing data, download the processed PsychAD count matrices and metadata from Zenodo (linked above under Sample data) and point the relevant numbered folder's scripts at your local copy — check that folder's script for the expected file paths/structure, since input conventions can differ slightly between folders given they were developed for different stages of the analysis.

For the compositional analysis specifically (folders 4 and 6), note that the paper uses centered-log-ratio (CLR) transformed cell-type fractions via crumblr rather than raw proportions, which matters if you're trying to match their exact statistics rather than just get a qualitative sense of compositional shifts.
tutorial_output: Each numbered folder reproduces one part of the paper rather than a single unified output: folder 2 outputs cell-type taxonomy assignments (class/subclass/subtype labels per nucleus); folders 3-4 output variance-partitioning tables and compositional fold-change statistics per cell subclass; folder 5 outputs differential expression gene lists (with effect sizes and posterior probabilities from the multivariate Bayesian meta-analysis) per disorder and cell type; folder 7 outputs the trained disease-trajectory neural network models along with per-gene trajectory module assignments (early/late-increasing/decreasing); and folder 8 outputs the heritability-transcriptome concordance statistics. Check the relevant subfolder's own scripts/README for exact file formats, since this varies by module.

sample_data.text: Full processed snRNA-seq data for the PsychAD cohort, hosted on Zenodo.

title: NeMoS (NEural MOdelS) — a JAX-powered statistical modeling framework for systems neuroscience
authors: Balzani E., NeMoS Developers (Flatiron Institute Center for Computational Neuroscience)
summary: NeMoS is a JAX-powered, GPU-accelerated Python toolbox for fitting generalized linear models (GLMs) to neural spike-count or continuous time-series data, with a composable basis-function module for feature engineering (splines, raised-cosine bases, convolutional filters) and multiple regularization schemes (Ridge, Lasso, GroupLasso, ElasticNet).
abstract_long: Unlike most entries here, NeMoS isn't tied to a single research paper — it's a general-purpose, actively maintained statistical modeling library from the Flatiron Institute's Center for Computational Neuroscience, cited via its Zenodo software record rather than a journal article. It has two core modules: a "basis" module that turns raw covariate time series (stimuli, position, head direction, LFP phase, spike counts, etc.) into model features, either through non-linear basis expansions (B-splines, M-splines, raised-cosine bases) or through convolution with a bank of temporal filters; and a "glm" module that fits single-neuron (GLM) or population-wide (PopulationGLM) generalized linear models to those features, with a choice of observation model (Poisson, Negative Binomial, Gamma, Gaussian, Bernoulli) and regularizer (Ridge, Lasso, GroupLasso, ElasticNet). It's designed to pair naturally with pynapple for upstream data handling, and its GPU acceleration via JAX makes it practical to fit these models at population scale.
data_acquisition: Not applicable — general-purpose statistical modeling toolbox for any spike-count or continuous time-series data (works with whatever neurophysiology or behavioral recordings you already have)
animal: Not applicable — general-purpose framework, not species- or acquisition-specific
tutorial_intro: NeMoS is a general-purpose Python package rather than a tool built around one specific file format — it works on whatever time-series arrays you already have (typically spike counts as the response variable, and behavioral/stimulus covariates as predictors), as plain numpy arrays or as pynapple time-series objects if your recording has natural epoch boundaries (separate trials or sessions with gaps).
tutorial_steps: Install: pip install nemos (macOS/Linux) or python -m pip install nemos (Windows).

Turn your raw covariates into model features using a basis object. For a smooth non-linear mapping use something like nmo.basis.MSplineEval(n_basis_funcs=5); for capturing temporal dynamics via a filter bank, use a convolutional basis like nmo.basis.RaisedCosineLogConv(n_basis_funcs, window_size=...). Basis objects are composable — you can combine several with * (multiplicative interaction) and + (additive) to build a compound feature set from multiple covariates.
Call .compute_features(...) on your (possibly compound) basis object, passing in your raw input time series (stimulus, position, LFP phase, population spike counts, etc.), to get the design matrix X.

Fit a GLM: nmo.glm.GLM().fit(X, y) for a single neuron's spike-count series y, or nmo.glm.PopulationGLM().fit(X, spike_counts) to jointly fit an entire simultaneously-recorded population. Optionally specify an observation model (Poisson is the default; also Negative Binomial, Gamma, Gaussian, Bernoulli) and a regularizer (Ridge, Lasso, GroupLasso, ElasticNet) when instantiating the GLM.

Inspect the fit via glm.coef_ and glm.intercept_ (the learned weights), glm.predict(X) (predicted firing rate), and glm.score(X, y) (log-likelihood) — the standard building blocks for interpreting an encoding model or comparing model variants.

If your data has natural epoch boundaries (separate trials or sessions with gaps between them), format it as a pynapple time-series first — the basis module's convolution step then runs epoch-by-epoch automatically, avoiding artifacts from those gaps.
tutorial_output: Fitted GLM coefficients and an intercept describing each feature's contribution to firing rate, a predicted firing-rate time series from predict(), and a log-likelihood score from score() — the standard outputs of a statistical encoding model, from which you'd typically derive tuning curves, compare nested models, or evaluate goodness of fit.

title: MEDiCINe: Motion Estimation by Distributional Contrastive Inference for Neurophysiology
authors: Watters N., Buccino A.P., Jazayeri M.
summary: MEDiCINe estimates brain motion (drift) during electrophysiology recordings by jointly optimizing two components — a motion function and an activity distribution along the probe — via gradient descent on detected spike amplitudes, depths, and times. It plugs directly into SpikeInterface and Kilosort4 pipelines, requires no manual parameter tuning across dozens of NHP datasets, and produces motion estimates as simple numpy arrays.
abstract_long: Probe drift during extracellular recordings distorts spike waveforms and degrades spike sorting quality. MEDiCINe addresses this by decomposing neural activity data into two jointly-optimized components: a motion function m(t, depth) describing how the brain moves relative to the probe over time and depth, and an activity distribution a(depth) describing the baseline firing rate distribution along the probe. These are fit simultaneously via gradient descent to maximize the likelihood of the observed spike amplitude-depth-time dataset. The motion function is parameterized as a smooth (triangular kernel-smoothed) function with configurable temporal resolution (default 1s bins, 30s smoothing kernel) and depth bins (default 2, allowing linear interpolation of non-rigid motion). The activity distribution is parameterized as a small MLP. No labeled data is required — the model trains entirely on detected spikes from the session itself. The output is a motion array (time_bins x depth_bins) in microns that can be used directly with SpikeInterface's InterpolateMotionRecording or with Kilosort4's datashift module.
data_acquisition: Extracellular electrophysiology recordings from silicon probes (e.g. Neuropixels); input is detected spike amplitudes, depths, and times — not raw voltage traces — so MEDiCINe is agnostic to recording hardware and compatible with any upstream spike detection pipeline
animal: Not species-specific; validated on NHP recordings across dozens of sessions
tutorial_intro: MEDiCINe is installed as medicine-neuro from PyPI. The single entry point is medicine.run_medicine(), which takes spike amplitudes, depths, and times as numpy arrays and writes motion estimates to an output directory. It does not process raw voltage — any upstream spike detector works. The most common use is as a drop-in motion correction step inside a SpikeInterface pipeline, but it also integrates with Kilosort4 directly.
tutorial_steps: Install and verify: pip install medicine-neuro python -m medicine_demos.run_demo The demo downloads a sample dataset and displays motion estimation figures.

Run motion estimation by passing detected spike times, depths, and amplitudes to medicine.run_medicine(). These can come from SpikeInterface peak detection, Kilosort, or any other detector: import medicine, numpy as np from pathlib import Path output_dir = Path("medicine_output") output_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) medicine.run_medicine( peak_amplitudes=..., peak_depths=..., peak_times=..., output_dir=output_dir, ) motion = np.load(output_dir / "motion.npy") time_bins = np.load(output_dir / "time_bins.npy") depth_bins = np.load(output_dir / "depth_bins.npy")

Apply motion correction in a SpikeInterface pipeline: from spikeinterface.core.motion import Motion from spikeinterface.sortingcomponents.motion.motion_interpolation import InterpolateMotionRecording motion_object = Motion( displacement=motion, temporal_bins_s=time_bins, spatial_bins_um=depth_bins, ) recording_corrected = InterpolateMotionRecording( recording, motion_object, border_mode="force_extrapolate" ) # Pass recording_corrected to your spike sorter with its built-in motion correction disabled

Check the figures saved to output_dir/, especially corrected_motion_raster.png. The defaults work for most datasets — the only parameters worth adjusting are motion_bound (increase if drift is very large), time_kernel_width (decrease if motion is fast), and amplitude_threshold_quantile (increase to exclude noisy low-amplitude spikes). See the README for the full parameter reference and Kilosort4 integration instructions.
tutorial_output: motion.npy: estimated probe motion in microns (n_time_bins x n_depth_bins). time_bins.npy and depth_bins.npy: corresponding bin centers. Diagnostic figures saved to output_dir including raw raster, motion overlay, and corrected raster.
